From hacera, from facera, from facero, from Latin faciarius, from faciēs (“face”).

Derived from Latin accommodātor. By surface analysis, acomodar + -ador.

parole.significato: to activate (to encourage development or induce increased activity; to stimulate)

parole.significato: to accumulate (to heap up in a mass)

parole.significato: accusatory (pertaining to, or containing, an accusation)

parole.significato: to adapt, to adjust, to tailor (to make suitable)

Borrowed from Latin crotalum (“castanet”), from Ancient Greek κρόταλον (krótalon).

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin quadrātūra. It replaced the inherited forms cuadradura, quadradura. First appeared in this spelling in 1527.
Inherited from Old Spanish cuajo, from Latin coāgulum. Compare the borrowed doublet coágulo.

parole.significato: like, as, in the manner of

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish qualidat, from Latin qualitātem. Doublet of calidad.
Inherited from Latin quam. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís.
Inherited from Latin quandō. Compare English cue and when.

parole.significato: whatever quantity, as much, however much
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin quantus, from Proto-Italic *kʷijentos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂onts (“how much, how many”), from *kʷíh₂, neuter of *kʷís. Cognate with French quant, Italian quanto, Portuguese quanto, Romanian cât, Ashkun ćīt, Waigali kiti, Sanskrit कियत् (kíyat), Avestan 𐬗𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬧𐬙 (cuuaṇt).
Inherited from Old Spanish quaraenta, from Latin quadrāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥(d)ḱomt (“four-ten”).

parole.significato: cuarteron, Spanish quarterpound (a traditional unit of mass equivalent to about 115 g)
parole.testo: From cuarto (“one-fourth”) + -ón (-oon: forming related nouns), from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”). Cognate with Portuguese quarta.
From cuarto and cuarta (“fourth, quarter”) + -illa (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Latin quartus (“fourth”). Doublet of cuartillo.

parole.significato: cuartillo, quarter-celemin (a traditional unit of dry measure equivalent to about 1.2 L)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish quartillo (“little fourth”), from quarto + -illo (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”). Equivalent to cuarto (“fourth”) + -illo (“-elle: forming diminutives”). Doublet of cuartilla. Cognate with Galician cuartillo and Portuguese quartilho.
From Latin quartus. Doublet of cuarta. The sense of room is after a common division of houses (4 or 5 sections). As a unit of English measure, calque of English quart. Compare English quarter.
Borrowed from Latin quadrimestris with the prefix influenced by cuatro (“four”).

Inherited from Old Spanish quatro, from Latin quattŭor (“four”), from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Cognates include Ancient Greek τέσσαρες (téssares), French quatre, Old English feower (English four).
From Old Spanish cuadrupea, from Latin (animālia) quadrupedia "four-legged (animals)". The modern form presumably reflects influence from cuatro (“four”).
Inherited from Old Spanish cuba, from Latin cūpa, from Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“a hollow”). Doublet of copa, via the Latin variant cŭppa.

parole.significato: cube (a regular polyhedron having six identical square faces)
parole.testo: From Latin cubus, from Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos).

parole.significato: bucket, pail (a container made of rigid material, often with a handle, used to carry liquids or small items)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cubrir, cobrir, from Latin cooperīre. Cognate with English cover.
Borrowed from Latin cubiculum (“bedroom; bedchamber”), from cubō (“to lie down, to sleep”). Doublet of cobijo, which was inherited.

parole.significato: historic grain measure, roughly a third of a quartile

parole.testo: From cucho (“compost, manure”) + -ar, the first element being from Latin cultus (“cultivated, tilled”).

From cuchar, from Latin cochleāre (with an unusual development of /-kl-/, likely due to the early palatalization of /lj/>/ʒ/), from cochlea. Compare Portuguese colher, Catalan cullera, French cuillère, cuiller, Italian cucchiaio, Sicilian cucchiara.
From cuchillo, inherited from Latin cultellus.
Inherited from Old Spanish cuchiello, from Latin cultellus, a diminutive of culter. Cognate with English cutlery. Compare English cutlass also.

parole.significato: neck (part of body connecting the head and the torso)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cuello, from Latin collum. Cognate with English collar, French cou, Italian collo, Galician and Portuguese colo.
From Latin concha (“bivalve, vessel, trumpet”). Doublet of concha (“seashell, scoop”), which was inherited from the diminutive Latin conchula. Compare English conch.
From cuero (“leather”), inherited from Latin corium (“leather”). Doublet of cuirass.
Inherited from Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, cord”). Doublet of corda.
Backformed from an Old Spanish *cordado, from Latin cordātus. For the diphthong, compare Old Spanish cuer (“heart”).
Inherited from Latin cornū, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”).
Inherited from Latin corium (“skin; hide, leather”). Sense 4 probably as a euphemism for cuerpo (“body”).

parole.significato: body (the physical structure of a human or animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cuerpo, from Latin corpus. Doublet of corpus (a borrowing).
Inherited from Latin corvus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂wós.
Inherited from Latin costa (“rib; side, wall”), later coming to mean “edge” or “coast” in Medieval Latin. Compare the borrowed doublet costa.
Borrowed from Latin quaestiōnem. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English question.
Past participle of cuidar; corresponds to Latin cōgitātus. The Philippine sense is a calque of Tagalog bahala, as in the expressions bahala ka, ako bahala, ikaw bahala, etc.

parole.significato: to look after, take care of (e.g. a house, a person)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cuidar (“to think; to take care of”), from Latin cogitāre (“to think”). Doublet of cogitar, a learned borrowing from Latin, whence also English cogitate.
Inherited from Old Spanish culuebro, from Latin colubrum.
Learned borrowing from Latin culmen. Doublet of cumbre.

parole.significato: ass, arse, booty, rear, behind, butt, buttocks
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish culo, from Latin culus.
Learned borrowing from Latin culpa; cf. the inherited Old Spanish colpa.
From Latin cultūra (“culture”), from cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“to till, cultivate”).

parole.significato: summit, peak, top, hilltop (topmost point or surface, especially of a mountain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin culminem, from Proto-Italic *kolamen, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH-. The sense of “gathering” is a calque of English summit. Doublet of culmen.
From cumplir (“to comply, complete, do what is proper”) + -miento or from Latin complēmentum. Compare the borrowed doublet complemento.
Inherited from Old Spanish cuna, from Latin cūna, cūnae, from Proto-Italic *koinā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoyneh₂, derived from the root *ḱey- (“to be lying down; to settle”).
Inherited from Latin cūra (“care, concern”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
Inherited from Old Spanish curaçion (1385), borrowed from Latin cūrātiōnem.

parole.significato: to care, heed, study, strive, seek, work

parole.testo: Uncertain. From older curueña, probably from an alteration of Latin columna (compare Old Occitan coronna, Milanese corogna), but probably influenced by cuero (as the carriages of crossbows were originally made of this material). Compare columna, which may be a doublet.

parole.significato: curriculum vitae, CV (written account of one's education, accomplishments etc.)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin curriculum vītae (“course of life”).

parole.significato: curriculum (set of courses and content offered by an educational institution)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin curriculum. Compare carrejo, possibly an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin cursus. See also coso, a doublet inherited from the same origin.
Borrowed from Latin curvāre, probably borrowed; cf. corvar and encorvar.
Learned borrowing from Latin curvus (“bent”). Doublet of corvo, which was inherited.

Inherited from Old Spanish cuyo, from Latin cuius, genitive of quī (“who, which”, interrogative and relative pronoun). Secondarily developed grammatical agreement with the thing possessed, thereby becoming a determiner rather than a pronoun in the strict sense. The grammatical agreement is attested
Inherited from Old Spanish qual, from Latin quālis (“which”).
Inherited from Latin quandō. Compare English cue.

From earlier quánto, from Latin quantus, from Proto-Italic *kʷijentos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂onts (“how much, how many”), from *kʷíh₂, neuter of *kʷís. Cognate with French quant, Italian quanto, Portuguese quanto, Romanian cât, Ashkun ćī́t, Waigali kiti, Sanskrit कियत् (kíyat), Avestan 𐬗𐬎𐬎𐬀
Inherited from Latin corrugus, from Paleo-Hispanic.
Inherited from Latin cophinus (“hamper, basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”). Compare Portuguese côvão, Italian cofano, French coffre. Doublet of cofre.

Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Latin cognātus. Doublet of the semi-learned borrowing cognado. The "know-all" sense alludes to the stereotypical behavior of brothers-in-law at Christmas celebrations, weddings and family gatherings.
Inherited from Latin cuneus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱū (“sting”). Compare Sicilian cugnu.

parole.significato: a reed pen, used to write with ink in antiquity
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calamus (“reed, cane”). Compare Spanish carámbano, inherited from a diminutive form of the Latin.
From Latin calathus, from Ancient Greek κάλαθος (kálathos). Doublet of calaje.
Borrowed from Latin calculus (“pebble”), diminutive of calx (“limestone”), from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix, “pebble”).
Borrowed from Latin calidus (“warm, hot”). Compare the doublet caldo. Cognate with English calid.
Borrowed from Latin calicem. Doublet of cauce.
Borrowed from Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux).
From Latin cammarus (“lobster”), from Ancient Greek κάμμαρος (kámmaros), καμμαρίς (kammarís, “lobster”).
Borrowed from Latin cancer. Compare cangrejo, inherited from a Vulgar Latin diminutive form.
Borrowed from Latin candĭdus.; compare English candid.
From Latin cantharus (“cantharus”), from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos).
Borrowed from Latin canticum (“song, chanted passage in a comedy”), from cantus (“song”), from canō (“to sing”).

parole.significato: cannula (flexible tube used to feed or drain liquids or to provide oxygen)
capsule (small container containing a dose of medicine)

parole.testo: From cárcavo, from cácabo, itself from Latin caccabus (“cooking pot”).
From earlier cácavo, cácabo, inherited from Latin cāccabus (“cooking pot”).
Inherited from Old Spanish carcel, from Latin carcerem. The feminine gender is analogous.
Borrowed from Latin cathedra from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). Doublet of the inherited cadera.
From Latin caustĭcus, from Ancient Greek καυστικός (kaustikós).
Borrowed from Latin celeber (“celebrated”), of uncertain origin.
Learned borrowing from Latin celer, celerem.
Borrowed from Latin caelicus (“celestial, heavenly”), from caelum (“heaven; sky”); see cielo.

parole.significato: Celtic (of the Celts; of the style of the Celts)
cell (the basic unit of a living organism)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cēreus. Doublet of cirio, which was inherited.
A learned formation from the root of Latin cervus and the suffix -ido.
Borrowed from Latin cervīcem. Doublet of the inherited cerviz.
Inherited from Old Spanish céspede, from Latin cēspitem, cēspes, monophthongized variant of caespes.
Borrowed from Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós). By surface analysis, ciclo + -ico.
Learned borrowing from Latin cingulum. Doublet of cincho.
Borrowed from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós), probably from the name of the Cynosarges, a public gymnasium in Athens where Antisthenes taught.
Borrowed from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of guitarra and cedra, the former entered through Arabic, and the latter was inherited from a Vulgar Latin variant.
Borrowed from Latin cytisus. Doublet of codeso.
Inherited from Old Spanish çitola (c. 1250), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin cithara. Compare with French citole. Doublet of cítara, guitarra, and cedra.

parole.significato: cochlea (the complex, spirally coiled, tapered cavity of the inner ear)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cochlea, from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “spiral, snail shell”).
From Latin cōdicem. Cognate with English codex.

From Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra), from χολή (kholḗ, “bile”). The meaning of "anger" comes from the ancient medical concept of humourism in which a person with too much yellow bile is choleric (“easily becomes angry”).
From Latin colicus from Ancient Greek κωλικός (kōlikós), from κῶλον (kôlon, “colon”).
From Latin cōmicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós). Doublet of cómic.
Inherited from Latin cōmō̆, a non-literary form of quōmodo.
Borrowed from Latin computus. Doublet of cuento, which was inherited.

parole.significato: conclave (a closed meeting in which the elector cardinals of the Roman Catholic Church choose a new pope)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin conclāve. The shift in stress is due to analogy with such words as cóncavo and cónyuge.
From Latin condylus, from Ancient Greek κόνδυλος (kóndulos).

parole.significato: consul (official residing in major foreign towns to represent and protect the interests of the merchants and citizens o…
cosmic (of or from or pertaining to the cosmos or universe)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cosmicus, from Ancient Greek κοσμικός (kosmikós), from κόσμος (kósmos, “world, universe”).
Borrowed from Latin cubitum. Compare the inherited doublet codo. Cognate with English cubit.
Learned borrowing from Latin cumulus. Compare the inherited doublet colmo.
Inherited from Latin dātus. See dar.
Inherited from Latin dator. By surface analysis, dar + -dor.
Inherited from Old Spanish dar (“to give”), from Latin dare.
Borrowed from Latin datum. Cf. dado.

parole.significato: to damage, to harm, to hurt, to injure
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish dannar, from Latin damnāre. Cognate with English damn.

parole.significato: damaging, harmful, detrimental (especially in regards to animals)
parole.testo: From dañar + -ino, derived from Latin damnāre. Compare Portuguese daninho.
Inherited from Old Spanish danno, from Latin damnum, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnom (“expense, investment”). Cognate with English damage, also the related archaic dañaje.
Inherited from Latin damnōsus, equivalent to daño + -oso.

parole.significato: of; 's; used after the thing owned and before the owner
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁. Cognate with Ladino de.

parole.significato: in fact, actually, indeed, as a matter of fact
parole.testo: Calque of Latin de facto. Compare similar constructions with French de fait, Romanian de fapt, and Italian difatti (literally “of facts”).
Borrowed from Latin dē industriā. In Spanish, the literal meaning is “of industry”.
From Latin dē iūre (literally “according to law”).

Inherited from Old Spanish de nuevo (“again”), from Latin dē (“from”) + novō (“new”), possibly a restructured inherited form of Classical Latin dēnuō (“again, anew”), itself a reduced form of a supposed and unattested Old Latin *dē novōd. Related to Medieval Latin dē novō (“afresh, as a new thing, o
From Latin dērepente (“suddenly”). Equivalent to de (“of”) + repente (“a sudden act or occurrence”).

parole.significato: to mosey, to amble, to wander, to roam
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin deambulāre. Compare obsolete English deambulate.
Inherited from Old Spanish dever, from Latin dēbēre (“owe”). Cognates include English due and debt.
Borrowed from Latin dēbilitātiōnem. First attested in early 15th c..
Inherited from Old Spanish debilitar (1380), borrowed from Latin dēbilitāre.
Borrowed from Latin decachordum, from Ancient Greek δεκάχορδος (dekákhordos, “ten-stringed”), from δέκα (déka, “ten”) + χορδή (khordḗ, “guts, string of a musical instrument”).
From Latin decēnārius. Cognate with French décénaire, Italian decenario, Portuguese decenário.
Inherited from Latin dictātum (“precept, teaching”). Doublet of dictado.
Clipping of décimo, from Latin decimus.

parole.significato: to decide, to make up one's mind, to determine, to choose to

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“fall down”).

parole.significato: to say, to tell, to name, to mention
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish dezir, from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).
Inherited from Old Spanish declarar, from Latin dēclārāre. Cognate with English declare.
Borrowed from Latin dēclīnātiōnem (“declension”), from dēclīnō (“decline”) + -ātiō.
Borrowed from Latin dēclīvem. First attested c. 1500.
From Latin decorare (“to adorn, distinguish, honor”).
This form was borrowed from Latin decrēscere. Cf. also the older form, which may be an internal formation.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin dēcrēscentem. Compare Spanish creciente.
Borrowed from Latin dēcrēmentum. The variant was formed internally.
Borrowed from Latin decagōnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek δεκάγωνος (dekágōnos), from δεκα- (deka-) + γωνίᾱ (gōníā) + -ος (-os).

parole.significato: digit: finger or toe, literally translated as "finger" and thought of that way by Spanish-speaking learners of English
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish dedo, from Latin digitus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”). Doublet of dígito, which was borrowed rather than inherited. Cognate with Catalan dit, Galician and Portuguese dedo, French doigt, Italian dito, Romanian deget.

parole.significato: to deduce, to deduct, to infer

parole.testo: From Latin dēfecāre, infinitive of defecō.
Inherited from Old Spanish defecçion (c. 1250), borrowed from Latin dēfectiōnem.

parole.significato: to defend, to protect, to hold down
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish defender, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin dēfendere. Cognate with English defend.
Borrowed from Latin dēfēnsāre (“to defend”), from dēfēndō.
Inherited from Old Spanish deferir (c. 1240), borrowed from Latin deferō. Cognate with English defer.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēficientia. Compare Catalan deficiència, French déficience, Italian deficienza, Portuguese deficiência.

parole.significato: definition (a statement of the meaning of a word)
to deflagrate (to burn with intense light and heat)
to deflower, to take away the sexual virginity
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēflōrāre, present active infinite of dēflōrō (“to deprive of flowers”), from dē (“from, away”) + flōs, flōris (“flower”).
Borrowed from Latin deformāre, or from de- + formar.
Borrowed from Latin dēfōrmitātem (“deformity, ugliness”), from dēfōrmis (“deformed, ugly”) + -itās, from dē + fōrma (“shape, form”).
From Latin degenerātiōnem; degenerar + -ción; cognate with Galician dexeneración and Portuguese degeneração.
Inherited from Latin decollāre (“to decapitate or behead”), from dē- + collum (“neck, throat”) + -ō (compare Spanish cuello). Cognate with English decollate.

parole.significato: to inform on, squeal, to rat out
parole.testo: From Latin delātus. Cognate with Scottish dialectal English delate. Also, compare English defer.
Inherited from Old Spanish delectaçion (c. 1293), borrowed from Latin dēlectātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin delegātiōnem, from delego, equivalent to delegar + -ción.
Borrowed from Latin delphīnātus, from delphīnus (“dauphin”) + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, delfín + -ato. Doublet of delfinado and Delfinado.

Borrowed from Latin delphīnem, variant of delphīnus (compare French dauphin, Italian delfino), from Ancient Greek δελφίν (delphín), a later form of δελφίς (delphís, “dolphin”), from δελφύς (delphús, “womb”).
Inherited from Latin dēlicātus and doublet of delicado. Compare also English delicate.
From Latin deliberātiōnem, equivalent to deliberar + -ción.
Borrowed from Latin delicātus. Doublet of delgado.
Borrowed from Latin deliciōsus. Cognate with English delicious, French délicieux, Italian delizioso, Portuguese delicioso, Romanian delicios.
From Latin dēlīrium, from dēlīrāre (“to deviate from the path”). Equivalent to delirar + -io.
Borrowed from Latin dēlīctum. Cognate with English delict.
Inherited from Old Spanish demandar, from Latin demandāre.
Borrowed from Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρατία (dēmokratía), equivalent to demo- + -cracia.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin dēmōlīrī (“to demolish”). Cognate with English demolish.
Borrowed from Latin daemonium, from Ancient Greek δαιμόνιον (daimónion), diminutive of δαίμων (daímōn, “god, divine power”).
Inherited from Latin dē magis; compare Portuguese demais and Asturian demás. Equivalent to de- + más. From Latin magis (“more”) derivative magister comes also English master.
Borrowed from Latin dēnārius. Doublet of the inherited dinero.
Inherited from Latin deinde (“from there”). The preposition is influenced by, or conflated with, desde. Corominas and Pascual also propose the term is a conflation of Old Spanish desende and desde.
Borrowed from Latin denegātiōnem, from dēnegō.
Inherited from Old Spanish denegar, from Latin dēnegāre.

parole.significato: to be brave, to dare, to strive
parole.testo: From Latin denōtare. Doublet of denotar.

parole.significato: to name; to call; to designate

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dehonestō (“to disgrace, dishonor”).
Borrowed from Latin dēnotāre. Doublet of denodarse.
Learned borrowing from Latin denticulum. First attested c. 1527.

parole.significato: to depend, to be subject to
to remove hair from the body; to depilate

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dēpōnere. By surface analysis, de- + poner.

parole.significato: to deposit, to put, to place
parole.testo: From Latin depono (Present active infinitive Dēpōnere).
From Latin dēprecārī (“to avert, ward off, deprecate”).
From Latin dēpositum. Compare English deposit.
From the feminine of derecho, from Latin directus; compare Portuguese direita, Catalan dreta, French droite, Italian dritta, Romanian dreapta.
Learned borrowing from Latin dērelictus. Doublet of derrelicto.
From redor, from Latin retrō. The initial "d-" is possibly from de.
Borrowed from Latin dērelictus. Doublet of derelicto.
Inherited from Old Spanish des-, from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís. Doublet of dis-, which was borrowed.
From des- + arrollar, from Latin dis- (“not”) + rotulus (“roll of paper”).
From des- + atornillar, from tornillo, from torno, from Latin tornus, from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos), from Proto-Indo-European *torh₂no-, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, bore, twist”).
From des- + archaic caecer (“to occur”), from Latin *cadescere.
Inherited from Old Spanish decender, decendir, borrowed from Latin dēscendere. Compare also the Old Spanish form deçir, which was likely inherited from the same source.
From des- + correr, possibly corresponding to Latin discurrere.
From de- + secar, or from Latin desiccāre.

parole.significato: to cast off, cast away, cast aside
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin disiectāre. By surface analysis, des- + echar.
Borrowed from Latin desertorem, from Latin desertus.
From a variant of Latin dēflōrāre, present active infinite of dēflōrō (“to deprive of flowers”), from dē (“from, away”) + flōs, flōris (“flower”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin dēsertus, probably taken as an early semi-learned term (the completely inherited/popular result would have been disierto, which was found in a few old texts).
Inherited from Old Spanish desierto, dessierto, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin dēsertum.
From Latin dēsignātiōnem, equivalent to designar + -ción.
Borrowed from Latin dēsignāre. Doublet of diseñar.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēlēre (“to destroy”), adapted to des-. Compare Portuguese delir and English delete.
Inherited from Latin delimitare. Equivalent to des- + lindar.
From des- + lumbre + -ar, from Latin lūmen (“light”).
From Latin disnūdāre, altered form of dēnūdāre, from dē + nūdus (“bare”). Compare Portuguese desnudar, French dénuer.
Ultimately from Latin nūdus, influenced by the verb desnudar or derived from it. Compare Portuguese desnudo, Occitan desnut.
Learned borrowing from Latin dēsōlātiō. Equivalent to desolar + -ción
Learned borrowing from Latin dēsōlāre, from dē- + sōlus (“alone”) + -ō (verbal suffix). Cognate with English desolate, French désoler, Italian desolare, Portuguese desolar, and Romanian dezolare.
Inherited from Latin dēspectāre (“despise”, literally “to look down upon”).

parole.significato: spite, resentment, envy, anger, indignation, dismay
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin dēspectus; cognate with English despite. By surface analysis, des- + pecho.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin dispēnsa, from dispēnsō (“to dispense, to distribute”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin disperditiōnem (“destruction, ruin”).
From Latin dē- + Vulgar Latin *expertus, for Latin experrēctus, past active participle of expergīscor (“to awaken”). Compare Portuguese desperto.

parole.significato: to strip, clear, leave bare, to despoil
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Latin dēspoliāre.
Pseudo-Latinism, derived from dēspōnsō (“to betroth”) + -torium (“instrument noun suffix”), equivalent to desposar + -torio.
Inherited from Latin dēstillāre (“to distil, trickle”). Compare the borrowed doublet destilar.
Borrowed from Latin dēstīllāre (“to distill, to trickle”). Compare the inherited doublet destellar.

From Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos). Compare English elenchus (“a Socratic method of debate”).

parole.significato: to elide (to cut off, as a vowel or a syllable)

parole.testo: From Latin ellipsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of elipsis.

Borrowed from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “falling short, omission”), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “to fall short, to leave out”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + λείπω (leípō, “to leave”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-. Doublet of elipse.

parole.significato: she, her (used subjectively and after prepositions)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illa, feminine of ille.

parole.significato: they, them (used subjectively and after prepositions; can refer to women and feminine nouns)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illās, accusative feminine plural of ille.

parole.significato: it, neuter third-person subject and disjunctive pronoun
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illud, neuter of ille. See also lo.
Borrowed from Latin ēloquentia, from ēloquens (“eloquent”).
From Latin ēlogium (“inscription on a tombstone”), the sense development being "inscription" > "recognition" > "praise".

parole.significato: to circumvent, to elude, to avoid, to evade, to escape, to get around
parole.testo: From Latin ēlūdere (“evade, elude”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + lūdō (“play; trick”).
From Latin elusor. By surface analysis, eludir + -or.
Borrowed from Latin hellebŏrum, from Ancient Greek ἑλλέβορος (helléboros), possibly from ἄλκη (álkē, “fawn”) and βιβρώσκω (bibrṓskō, “to eat”).

parole.significato: elliptical (in the shape of an ellipse; oval)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós, “defective”).

parole.significato: to absorb, to soak up, to imbibe

parole.testo: From Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “insertion”).
From en- + bracil (“vambrace”) + -ar, from Latin bracchialis (“arm”).
From Latin imbūtus (“moistened”), from imbuō (“to wet, moisten”).
From Latin impositum according to 1914’s DRAE, of unknown origin according to recent editions.
Inherited from Latin impetīgō. Doublet of the borrowed impétigo.
Inherited from Latin impellere. Compare the borrowed doublet impeler.
From Old Spanish emperador, from Latin imperātōrem.
From Scientific Latin empyema, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύημα (empúēma), from Ancient Greek πύον (púon, “pus”).
From earlier emplastro, from Latin emplastrum.
Borrowed from Latin emporium (“market”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπορεῖον (emporeîon), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “marketer”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πόρος (póros, “travel”).
From empujar + -ón, or possibly from Latin impulsiōnem (and if so, doublet of impulsión). Compare Portuguese empuxão.
Borrowed from Latin emulgēre (“to milk out, to drain out, to exhaust”).
Borrowed from Latin ēmungere (“to wipe or blow the nose”).

parole.significato: emeritus (retired but retaining an honorific version of previous title)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish en, from Latin in, from Old Latin en, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én.
Inherited from Old Spanish en-, from Latin in-, prefixation of Latin in (“in, into”); see en.

From en- + Old Spanish ajenar, inherited from Latin aliēnāre, a verb based on aliēnus. Near-doublet of alienar, a borrowing from Latin. See Medieval Latin inalienare, from Latin in- + alienāre. Compare Sicilian allianari.
From Latin nānus, from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos). Cognate with Portuguese anão. Compare English nano-.
From en- + cana + -ecer or from Latin incānēscere.
Possibly a semi-learned borrowing from Latin incantāre. By surface analysis, en- + cantar.
Learned borrowing from Latin incarcerāre. By surface analysis, en- + cárcel + -ar.
Inherited from Latin incendere. Cognate with English incense.
From encetar (with influence from comenzar), from Latin inceptāre.
Inherited from Latin incīnctus, perfect passive participle of incingō. Compare Italian incinto, French enceint.
Inherited from Old Spanish en- + comendar, from Latin commendāre. Compare comandar, a doublet borrowed from Italian or French.
From Latin in contra. Compare Portuguese encontrar, Italian incontrare, and French rencontrer.
Inherited from Latin incurvāre. Cognate with English incurve.
Inherited from Old Spanish enzia, from Latin gingīva, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
From Latin endocrinus, itself from endo- + Ancient Greek κρίνειν (krínein, “to separate”).
From Latin endometrium, from endo- and Ancient Greek μήτρα (mḗtra).

parole.significato: to harden, to toughen, make hard
parole.testo: From Latin indūrēscere, from indūrō. By surface analysis, en- + duro + -ecer.

parole.significato: enema (injection of fluid into the rectum)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin enema, from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).
Inherited from Old Spanish enemigo (“fiend”), from Latin inimīcus, from amīcus (“friend”).
Borrowed from Latin energīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).
From Latin energūmenus. Compare English energumen.
From Latin īnfirmitātem (“weakness”), from īnfirmus (“weak, feeble”), equivalent to enfermo + -edad.
Inherited from Latin īnfirmus (“weak, feeble”), from īn- + firmus (“strong”).

parole.significato: to make thin, weaken, emaciate (to cause to become extremely thin or wasted)
parole.testo: From en- + flaco (“thin”) + -ecer, from Latin flaccus.
Inherited from Latin ingenium. Doublet of ingenio.
From Spanish prefix en- + Latin gradī, equivalent to Latin ingredī. Compare English ingress.

Inherited from Old Spanish enfiesto, most likely inherited from Latin īnfestus. For the semantic development, Coromines and Pascual point out the use of īnfestus in classical Latin to describe spears in attack position and standards during marches, a usage that survives into Old Spanish alongside th
From Latin aenigma (“riddle”), from Ancient Greek αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, riddle”).
From Latin exāminātiō, from Latin exāmen. Doublet of examinación, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Old Spanish ensamne (“swarm, beehive”), from Latin exāminem, singular accusative of exāmen (“swarm”). Doublet of examen, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin exsūcāre, with the prefix ex- being replaced in Spanish by en-.
Inherited from Old Spanish enxundia, from Latin axungia.

Inherited from Old Spanish enxuto, from Latin exsūctus, perfect passive participle of exsūgō, from ex + sūgō. Compare Portuguese enxuto, Catalan eixut, Italian asciutto. In pre-literary Spanish, the word likely had the form *eissuito (compare also Old Galician-Portuguese enxoyto, Galician enxoito),
An early borrowing from Latin ēmendāre. Reformulated after the common prefix en-.
Borrowed from Latin ēnormitātem. By surface analysis, enorme + -idad.
Feminine form of ensenado (“having the form of a sound or inlet”) from en- + seno (“sound, sinus, breast”) from Latin sinus.
From Latin īnsignia; an inheritance or (probably more likely) a semi-learned borrowing.
From en- + Latin surdēscere, from surdus (“deaf”) + -ēscō. Alternatively, from en- + sordo + -ecer. Compare Portuguese ensurdecer, Catalan ensordir.
Inherited from Old Spanish entender (“to fathom”), from Latin intendere, from in- + tendō. Doublet of intender, a borrowing.
From en- + Latin tenebrēscere (“to darken, to become dark”) (a borrowing), from tenebrae (“darkness”). Compare inherited Spanish tinieblas.

Either from entero, or inherited from Latin integrāre (“to renew, restore, make whole”); compare doublets entregar (“to deliver”) (semi-learned) and integrar (“to make up, compose”) (a later learned borrowing). Compare English integrate.

Inherited from Latin integrum (“entire, whole”). Compare also the semi-learned forms found in medieval Spanish entegro, entrego, and the later learned borrowing íntegro. Cognate with English entire and integer.
From a derivative of Latin intēnsus, possibly through a Vulgar Latin *intēnsāre; compare Portuguese entesar, Occitan entesar, Old French entaisier. See also tieso.

parole.significato: then, next, thereupon, at that time, at that point
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish entonce, entonces, from Latin in + *tunce, the latter an archaic form of tunc (“then”). Compare Portuguese então and Romanian atunci.

parole.significato: to enter; to come in; to get in; to go in; to get inside; to come on in
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish entrar, from Latin intrāre. Cognate with English enter.

Inherited from Latin interānea, from the plural of interāneum (“gut, intestine”), substantive of interāneus (“internal, inward”). Compare Portuguese entranha, Catalan entranya, French entrailles and English entrails.
Inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).

parole.significato: between ourselves, between us, inter nos
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter nos. Morphologically equivalent to entre (“between”) + nos (“us”) (archaic, displaced by nosotros).
Inherited from Latin inter-. Doublet of inter-.
From Latin interdīcō. Doublet of interdecir.
Inherited from Latin interdictum. Compare the borrowed doublet interdicto.

parole.significato: to deliver, to hand over, to hand off
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish entregar, entegrar, semi-learned borrowing from Latin integrāre with metathesis (compare Old Spanish entrego). Doublet of integrar (“to integrate”) and enterar (“to inform; to find out”). Cognate with English integrate.

parole.significato: to die away, to fade away (to be extinguished)
parole.testo: From entre- + morir, from Latin intermŏri.
Inherited from Latin intertexere, equivalent to entre- + tejer.
Inherited from Latin intervenīre. Doublet of intervenir.

parole.significato: to meddle, to get involved, to pry, to interfere, to intrude
parole.testo: From Latin intromittere, from Latin intrōmittō (“to admit, to let in; to introduce”).

Borrowed from Latin intumēscere. According to Coromines & Pascual, first attested in Baltasar Gracián (17th century). The verb was partly affected by the inherited verb adormecer, producing some of the alternative forms shown above.
From Latin ēnumerātiōnem. By surface analysis, enumerar + -ción.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēnūntiāre (“to reveal, to express”).
Inherited from Latin invitāre. Doublet of invitar, which was borrowed.

parole.significato: back (the reverse side of a leaf, fabric etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin inversum. Doublet of inverso and anverso.
Learned borrowing from Latin epactae, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπακταί f pl (epaktaí, “intercalary days”), from ἐπακτός (epaktós, “brought on or in, added”).
Learned borrowing from Latin epanadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναδίπλωσις (epanadíplōsis, “doubling, folding”).
Borrowed from Latin epanalepsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπανάληψις (epanálēpsis), from ἐπαναλαμβάνω (epanalambánō), from ἐπί (epí) + ἀνά (aná) + λαμβάνω (lambánō).
Borrowed from Latin epicoenus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκοινος (epíkoinos), based on κοινός (koinós, “common”).
From Latin Epicurēus, from Ancient Greek ’Επικούρειος (’Epikoúreios), from ἐπίκουρος (epíkouros, “assisting, defending, ally”).
From Scientific Latin epididymus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδιδυμίς (epididumís).
From Latin epigastrium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγάστριον (epigástrion).
From Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma), from ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + γράμμα (grámma, “that which is written, letter”).
Borrowed from Latin epigrammatista, from epigramma.
Borrowed from Latin epigrammaticus, from epigramma.
Borrowed from Latin epinīcium, from Ancient Greek ἐπινίκιον (epiníkion, “victory ode”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + νίκη (níkē, “victory”).
Borrowed from Latin epistolāris, from epistola (“letter”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ, “message, letter”).

Borrowed from Latin epitaphium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιον (epitáphion, “funeral oration”), neuter form of ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “over the grave”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb, grave”).

Borrowed from Latin epithalamium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).
Borrowed from Latin epōdos, from Ancient Greek ἐπῳδός (epōidós), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, over, above”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Borrowed from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos).

Borrowed from Latin epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton), neuter form of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “added”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi, “to add on”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, to place”).
From Latin echīnus, from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).
Borrowed from Latin aequinoctiālis, from aequinoctium (“equinox”).
From Latin echinoderma (compare the phylum name Echinodermata), from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos, “hedgehog, sea urchin”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”).
Borrowed from Latin aequiparāre, an alternative form of aequiperō (“to put on a level with, compare, liken”).

parole.significato: to be equivalent, to correspond, to be tantamount to

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ārea. Compare the borrowed doublet área.
Borrowed from Latin ērectus. Compare yerto.
From dialectal ería (“large section of cultivated and uncultivated fenced-in land”) + -al; from Latin ārea (“area, plot of land”).
Borrowed from Latin ērigere. Doublet of erguir, which was inherited. Compare English erect.
From Scientific Latin erythema, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma).
From Latin errāre. Related to English and Spanish error.
Calque of Latin errare humanum est.
Borrowed from Latin errāta (“mistaken things, mistakes”), neuter plural of errātus (“mistaken”). Compare yerro and error.
Probably borrowed from another Ibero-Romance language, from Latin ervilia. Doublet of arveja, the inherited Castilian form.
From Latin erōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós), from ἔρως (érōs, “sexual love, desire”).
Inherited from Old Spanish es-, from Latin ex- (“out of”). Doublet of ex-, which is borrowed.
Borrowed from Latin ēsca. Compare the inherited doublet yesca.

parole.significato: to sneak out, slip away, slip out
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin excapulāre, from Late Latin capulāre, from Latin capulum, from capiō. Compare the Italian scapolare.
From Latin scaphoides, from Ancient Greek σκαφοειδές (skaphoeidés), from Ancient Greek σκάφη (skáphē, “boat”) and Ancient Greek ειδές (eidés, “similar to”).

parole.significato: ladder (a frame, usually portable, of wood, metal, or rope, used for ascent and descent)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin scāla. Cognates include French échelle.
From escala + -ar or from Latin scalāris.
From Latin ascalōnia cēpa (“onion from Ashkelon”). Doublet of chalote.
From Old Spanish escama, from Latin squāma. Cognate with English squama and squame.
From escama + -ar; partly derived from Latin dēsquamāre.
Inherited from Latin squāmōsus. By surface analysis, escama + -oso. Compare English squamous.

parole.significato: scapular (a short cloak, now often with an embroidered image of a saint)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish escapulario (early 13th c.), Latin scapulāris (“of the back”).

parole.significato: to paw, scratch, scrape, dig (the ground)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish escarvar, from Latin scarīfāre, from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”). Cognate with English scarify, Galician escarvar.
Inherited from Latin excavāre. Equivalent to es- + cavar. Doublet of excavar.

parole.significato: seat (membership in an organization, particularly a representative body)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin scamnum, from Proto-Italic *skaβnom, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ-no-m, from *skabʰ- (“to hold up”). Cognate with Galician escano, Portuguese escano, Italian scanno, and more distantly Sanskrit स्कम्भ (skambhá).
Borrowed from Latin sca(e)na, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

parole.significato: to clarify, to come to light
parole.testo: From es- + clarecer, from Latin clārēscere.
From Scientific Latin sclērodermia, from Ancient Greek σκληρόδερμος (sklēródermos, “hard-skined”) + -ia.
Inherited from Old Spanish escoba, from Latin scōpa. Compare Italian scopa.
Inherited from Old Spanish escozer, from Latin excoquere (“to boil, melt”). Equivalent to es- + cocer.

parole.significato: to hew stones with an edged hammer
parole.testo: Uncertain, but possibly from Latin excutere (“shake off”), with a change in conjugation. Possibly related to Latin cos.

parole.significato: to go through a narrow place

parole.testo: From Latin scoliōsis, derived from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis), from σκολιός (skoliós, “twisted”) + -sis.

parole.significato: any of various centipedes of the genus Scolopendra
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scolopendra, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra).
Borrowed from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολαστικός (skholastikós, “scholarly, studious”).
Borrowed from Latin scombrī (“mackerel”), from Ancient Greek σκόμβρος (skómbros).

Inherited from Old Spanish esconder, from an original asconder (with a replacement of the prefix with es-), from Latin abscondere. It formerly showed the expected diphthongization of stressed short Latin /o/ in rhizotonic conjugations (see older escuendo), but this was later levelled out by analogy
Inherited from Old Spanish escopro, from Latin scalprum. Compare Portuguese escopro.
From Latin scorpiōnem, accusative singular of scorpiō.
Borrowed from Latin scriba. Doublet of escribano.
Inherited from Latin scriptor, scriptōrem. By surface analysis, escrito + -or.
Inherited from Old Spanish escritura (compare also the learned form scriptura), from Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scrōtum. First attested in the 18th century.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin scrūpulōsus. By surface analysis, escrúpulo + -oso.

parole.significato: scruple (doubt concerning the morality of some action)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin scrūpulus. Cognate with Portuguese escrópulo, escrúpulo.

parole.significato: to listen to, to hear out
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish escuchar, ascuchar, from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of auscultar, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Old Spanish escudiella, from Latin scutella, a diminutive form of scutra (“tray, dish, platter”).
Inherited from Old Spanish escudo, from Latin scūtum, from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”), an extension of *sek- (“to cut”). Cognate with English écu, scudo and escudo.

parole.significato: school (an institution dedicated to teaching and learning)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “spare time, leisure”, later “conversations and the knowledge gained through them during free time; the places where these conversations took place”).

Uncertain. One theory is Latin scorteus (“leathern”), referring to the wrinkled skin of a toad. Another possibility is a derivative of a Vulgar Latin *excurtiō, from Late Latin curtiō (“viper”), from Latin curtus (“short”) (thus cognate or linked with Catalan escurçó, dialectal Italian scorzone, Moz

parole.significato: sculpture (work of art created by sculpting)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish escorrer, from Latin excurrere (whence English excursion). Cf. also Portuguese escorrer, Asturian escorrer, Galician escorrentar.

Inherited from Old Spanish escusar, from Latin excūsāre. Cf. the modified form excusar. The meaning in this word was influenced by escuso (“hidden”), the old past participle of esconder (“to hide”), corresponding to Latin abscōnsus; cf. also escusa.
Borrowed from Latin scepticus, from Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós, “thoughtful, inquiring”), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to consider”).
Borrowed from Latin Sphingem, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphaericus. By surface analysis, esfera + -ico.
From Latin spatiōsitās, from spatiōsus (“spacious, roomy”). By surface analysis, espacioso + -idad. Compare Portuguese espaçosidade.
From Latin spatiōsus. By surface analysis, espacio + -oso.

parole.significato: sword (a long bladed weapon with a grip and typically a pommel and crossguard (together forming a hilt), which is desig…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish espada, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of espata.
Past participle of esparcir, from Latin spargere.

parole.significato: to scatter, disperse; to sprinkle; to fire out
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin spargere, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”). Cognate with English sparge. Also compare English sparse.

Inherited from Latin spartum (“esparto or halfah grass”), from Ancient Greek σπάρτον (spárton, “rope, cable; esparto or halfah grass”), valued for its high tensile strength, used for cords and wicker, and exported by Spanish Greek colonies throughout the Mediterranian. Cognate to Spanish espuerta.
From Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós).
From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”). Doublet of espada.

parole.significato: show, performance (play, dance, some act or series of acts of public entertainment, often live)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spectaculum. Cognate with English spectacle.

parole.significato: speculator, profiteer, scalper, (UK) stag, (oil, US) wildcatter
spelt (a type of wheat, Triticum spelta or Triticum aestivum subsp. spelta)
to creep, to frighten, to horrify
parole.testo: According to Corominas and Pascual, from earlier espeluzrar, from a blend of espeluzar + lazrar; the first element is likely from es- + peluza + -ar (variant of pelusa (“fluff, lint”)), while the second element is inherited from lacerāre.

Inherited from Old Spanish esperança, from Latin spērāns, from spērō, from Old Latin *spēsō, from spēs (“hope”) + -ō (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, esperar + -anza. Compare Portuguese esperança, Italian speranza, French espérance.
From Old Spanish esperar, from Latin spērō, -āre (“to hope, await”).
Inherited from Old Spanish espesso, from Latin spissus, from Proto-Indo-European *spidtos. Cognate with French épais.
Inherited from Old Spanish espiga, from Latin spīca.
Inherited from Old Spanish espina, from Latin spīna.
From espina (“thorn”), on the model of Latin spīnus (“blackthorn, sloe tree”).

parole.significato: a single turn of a spiral
parole.testo: From Latin spīra (probably borrowed), from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra).
Borrowed from Latin spirātiōnem. By surface analysis, espirar + -ción.

parole.significato: splendid, magnificent, splendiferous, superb, lavish, glorious

parole.testo: From Scientific Latin spondylitis, from spondy̆lus (“vertebra”), from Ancient Greek σπόνδυλος (spóndulos). Equivalent to espondilo- + -itis.

Inherited from Old Spanish esponja, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin spongia (compare the expected Old Spanish outcome *esponza), from Ancient Greek σπογγῐᾱ́ (spongĭā́), a later form of σπόγγος (spóngos, “sponge”). Doublet of espundia and hongo. Cognate with English sponge.

parole.significato: hamper, two-handled basket (a plaited basket with two handles, usually made from esparto grass or palm leaves)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sporta (“plaited basket, hamper”).
Inherited from Old Spanish espuma, from Latin spūma.

parole.significato: foamy; frothy; filled with or composed of bubbles
parole.testo: From espuma + -oso, or from Latin spūmōsus.

parole.significato: a type of ulcer afflicting horses and other equids.
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin spongia (“sponge”). Doublet of esponja. Compare Galician espulla (“wart; growth in cows”), also Romanian spânz (“horse disease”).
Borrowed from Latin spūtāre (“to spit out”), frequentative of spuō (“to spit”).
Borrowed from Latin spādīcem, from Ancient Greek σπάδιξ (spádix).
From Latin sparagus, asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
Learned borrowing from Latin specimen, from speciō (“observe, watch”) + -men (noun-forming suffix).
Learned borrowing from Latin speculum. Compare the inherited doublet espejo.
Borrowed from Latin spiritus. Compare the older forms espirto, espirtu. Cognate with English spirit.

Borrowed from Latin scheda (“piece of paper”), either borrowed directly or perhaps via Italian scheda, with Spanish speakers attempting to approximate the [-d-] with their own [-l-]. First documented in early modern Spanish.

parole.significato: outline (a general description, a summarizing statement)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).
From Latin schēmāticus, from Ancient Greek σχηματικός (skhēmatikós).
Inherited from Old Spanish estabile, estabele, estable, from Latin stabilis. Morphologically equivalent to estar + -able.
Inherited from Old Spanish establo, from Latin stab(u)lum.

parole.significato: to stable (to put in a stable)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish estacion, a learned borrowing from Latin statiō. Cognate with English station.
From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion).
Fossilized participle of estar (“to be”), from Latin stantem (“standing”), from Latin stāre (“to stand, stay”).

parole.significato: to be (have a temporary or permanent location in space)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish estar, from Latin stō, stare. The preterite's origin is unclear, most likely generalized from the preterite of haber (“to have”), hub- (note that b and v are pronounced identically; compare the same development in andar and tener and Portuguese estar). Preterite, imperfect
From Latin statuārius. By surface analysis, estatua + -ario.
Inherited from Old Spanish estanno, from Latin stannum, stagnum, of Celtic origin; compare Irish stán.
From Latin aestuāria, inflected form of aestuārium (“tidal basin, agitation of water”), from aestus (“tide”).

parole.significato: stele (upright slab containing engraved or painted decorations or inscriptions)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin stēla (“pillar”), from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē).

parole.significato: star; stellar (of or relating to stars)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stellāris. Doublet of estrellar.

parole.significato: floor mat (made of a thick, rustic fiber)
parole.testo: From older Old Spanish estuera, from Latin storea.
Borrowed from Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “brand, mark”), from στίζω (stízō, “to mark”).
Borrowed from Latin stylobata m, from Ancient Greek στυλοβάτης (stulobátēs), from στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”) + βαίνειν (baínein, “to go, to walk”).
Possibly from Latin aestimābilis, from aestimāre + -bilis.

parole.significato: dear (formal way of addressing somebody at the beginning of a letter)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stipulārī (“to stipulate”), possibly from stipula, or possibly from Proto-Italic *stipelāō.
From Latin aestivālis (“relating to the summer”), from aestīvus (“of the summer”), from aestus (“heat”).
Borrowed from Latin Stōicus, from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós), the portico in Athens where Zeno taught.
Inherited from Old Spanish estola (early 13th c.), from Latin stola, from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ, “stole, garment, equipment”).

parole.significato: stomach; stomachic (of or relating to the stomach)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish estopa, from Latin stuppa, from Ancient Greek στύππη (stúppē).
Inherited from Latin sturnīnus (“gray like a starling”), from sturnus (“starling”).
Inherited from Old Spanish estrado, from Latin strātum, strātus. Compare the borrowing estrato.
From Latin strāgem. Compare Galician and Portuguese estrago, and Italian strage. By surface analysis, deverbal from estragar.
Borrowed from Latin strangulāre (“to strangle”), from Ancient Greek στραγγαλάω (strangaláō, “to strangle”), variant of στραγγαλίζω (strangalízō), from στραγγάλη (strangálē, “a halter”).
From Latin stratēgēma, from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).
Derived from Latin strategia, from Ancient Greek στρᾰτηγῐ́ᾱ (strătēgĭ́ā).
Learned borrowing from Latin strātus. Compare the inherited estrado.
Inherited from Old Spanish estrecho, from Latin strictus. Doublet of estricto, a learned borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Latin strictūra. By surface analysis, estrecho + -ura.

Inherited from Old Spanish estrella, from Latin stēlla, probably through an unattested regional Latin *strēlla. Cognate with Asturian estrella, Catalan estrella, Galician estrela, and Portuguese estrela.

parole.significato: to shake, make tremble, make shudder
parole.testo: From ex- (“out of”) + tremiscere (“to start shaking”), from Latin tremō, whence English tremble and tremor.

parole.significato: gift, present given as a token of some pleasure, happiness, or benefit received
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin strēna. Compare Catalan estrena, Portuguese estreia and French étrenne.
Inherited from Old Spanish estrenuo, from Latin strenuus.

parole.significato: streptococcus (a spherical, gram-positive bacterium of the genus Streptococcus)
parole.testo: From Scientific Latin streptococcus, from Ancient Greek στρεπτός (streptós) and κόκκος (kókkos).
From Old Spanish estrennir, estrinnir, from Latin stringere (“to tighten”).
Learned borrowing from Latin strictus. Compare the inherited doublet Doublet of estrecho, which was inherited.

Pseudo-Latinism, derived from strīdēns (“uttering or making a shrill or harsh sound”) + -ia (“abstract noun suffix”), equivalent to estridente + -ia. Stridentia exists as a real word in Latin, but only as a form of the participle strīdēns. Cognate with Catalan estridència and Portuguese estridência.
Borrowed from Latin oestrus, from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros, “vehement desire, frenzy”, literally “gadfly”).
From Latin stropha, from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “turning”).
Perhaps from estopa (“tow, oakum”), from Latin stuppa (“tow, coarse flax”).
Borrowed from Latin aestuārium, from aestus (“tide”).
From estudio + -ar, from Latin studium. Compare English study, Latin studeō, Portuguese estudar.
Inherited from Old Spanish estudio, a learned borrowing from Latin studium. Related to estuche.
From Latin studiōsus. By surface analysis, estudio + -oso.
From Latin stupefaciō (“strike dumb, stun with amazement, stupefy”), from stupeō (“to be stunned”) + faciō (“to make”)
Inherited from Old Spanish estivo, from Latin [tempus] aestīvum (literally “summertime”).

parole.significato: stomach (an organ in animals that stores food in the process of digestion)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish estomago (“maw”), from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos, “gullet; stomach”), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).
Derived from Latin et cētera (literally “and the rest”).
Borrowed from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) + -λογία (-logía).
From Latin etymologus, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμόλογος (etumólogos).
Borrowed from Latin aethiopicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπικός (Aithiopikós). By surface analysis, Etiopía + -ico.

parole.significato: Euboean, Euboic (of, from or relating to Euboea (island in Greece))

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin euphorbium, from Ancient Greek εὐφόρβιον (euphórbion).
Borrowed from Latin eunuchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
Borrowed from Latin euthanasia, and this from Ancient Greek εὐθανασία (euthanasía).
Borrowed from Latin evanescere. Doublet of the inherited desvanecer.
From Latin evāsus, passive participle of evadĕre (“to elude, escape”), + -ivo.
From Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”) (shortened form of ex) + veniō (“come”).
By surface analysis, evento + -al. Ultimately based off Latin ēventuālis. The "eventual", "happening eventually" sense is a semantic loan from English eventual.
From Latin ēviscerāre (“to disembowel”), from ē- (“out”) + viscera (“bowels”) + -āre.
From Latin ēvītābilis. Cognate with rare English evitable. By surface analysis, evitar + -able.

parole.significato: to avoid, to bypass, to evade, to circumvent, to dodge, to shun, to eschew (to steer clear of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēvītāre whence English inevitable.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēvocāre (“to callout, summon”), from ex- (“out”) + vocāre (“to call”), from vōx (“voice”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin ex novo.

parole.significato: to exaggerate, to overstate, to overemphasize

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exāmen. Compare the inherited doublet enjambre.
Borrowed from Latin excavāre. Doublet of escavar.

Pseudo-Latinism, derived from excēdēns (“going out/forth/beyond”) + -ia (“abstract noun suffix”), equivalent to excedente + -ia. Excēdentia exists as a real word in Latin, but only as a form of the participle excēdēns. Cognate with Asturian escedencia, Catalan excedència, Italian eccedenza, and Port

parole.significato: to exceed (to be larger or greater than)

parole.testo: From Latin excellentem. Cognate with Italian eccellente, French excellent, English excellent.

Semi-learned alteration (based on the Latin etymon) of the inherited Old Spanish escusar, from Latin excūsāre. Cf. the now obsolete form escusar ("to hide"), influenced by the old past participle of esconder.

parole.significato: to demand; to require; to call for

parole.testo: From Latin exiguus (“strict, exact, scanty, meager”), from exigō (“to drive out”).
Borrowed from Latin eximō (“to release, to banish, to except”) (infinitive eximere).

parole.significato: to judge, to form an opinion

parole.testo: From Latin existere, infinitive of existō.
Borrowed from Latin exōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερικός (exōterikós), from ἐξωτέρω (exōtérō).
From Latin expānsiōnem. Cognate with English expansion.

Borrowed from Latin expectāre, variant of exspectō (“to wait”). Alternatively, possible backformation from expectante interpreted as a present participle, influenced as well by expectación and expectativa.

parole.significato: to issue, to publish (a document, etc)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin expedīre (“to release, to disconnect, to expedite, to prepare, to carry out, to send out”).

parole.significato: to sell (retail), to handle, deal in

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin expēnsās. Compare the inherited Old Spanish espesa.

parole.significato: esplanade, concourse (large, clear and level open space)
parole.testo: From older esplanada, from obsolete esplanar (“to flatten, to make level”), from Latin explānō (“to extend, to spread, to clarify, to explain”).
From Latin explānāre. Doublet of esplanar.

parole.significato: expletive (performing a syntactic role but contributing nothing to meaning)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin explicātor. By surface analysis, explicar + -dor.
From Latin explicātīvus, from explicō (“to unfold, open out”).

parole.significato: to pillage, to loot, to spoliate

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin expōnere. By surface analysis, ex- + poner.
From expreso + -ar, borrowed from Latin expressus.
From Latin exprimere. Was originally inherited (in its Old Spanish form espremir) and later modified in spelling to reflect the Latin etymology. Compare also the doublet expremir, rarely used today.

parole.significato: to assault, storm, take by storm

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin extendere, or modified from the Old Spanish estender, which may have been inherited.
Borrowed from Latin extēnsus, perfect passive participle of extendō (“extend, stretch out”).
Borrowed from Latin extenuātiōnem, accusative of extenuātiō.
From Latin exterminātor. By surface analysis, exterminar + -dor.

parole.significato: extinction (the action of making or becoming extinct; annihilation)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exstinctus or extinctus.
Borrowed from Latin extrā-, from extrā (“outside, beyond”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin extrahere, with conjugation modeled on traer. By surface analysis, ex- + traer.
Borrowed from Latin extraordinārius. Equivalent to extra- + ordinario.

parole.significato: strange, unusual, odd, weird, bizarre, uncanny, rare, peculiar, freaky, freakish, freak, curious
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish estranno, from Latin extrāneus, with /k/ originally lost and later reinserted according to the Latin form. Cognate with English extraneous and strange.
Derived from Latin ex vōtō (“from a vow”).

parole.significato: to ejaculate (have an orgasm); to cum

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fabella. Doublet of favela.
Borrowed from Latin fabricāre. Compare the inherited doublet fraguar.

parole.significato: fable, myth, legend; fabulous (of or relating to fable, myth, or legend)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fābulōsus (“celebrated in fable”).
Borrowed from Latin factiōnem. Doublet of fashion.
Learned borrowing from Latin faciēs. Doublet of faz and haz.
Borrowed from Latin facilitātem (“ease, easiness”), from facilis (“doable, easy”).
Borrowed from Latin factum. Compare the inherited doublet hecho.
Borrowed from Latin factor. Compare the inherited doublet hechor (cf. malhechor).

Borrowed from Latin factūra. Compare hechura, inherited from the same source. In the sense of a pastry, named by members of the Argentinian baker’s union to subversively call attention to the value of their labor.
Borrowed from Latin facundus. Compare Italian facondo.
Inherited from Latin favōnium. Doublet of favonio, which was borrowed.

parole.significato: phalanx (one of the bones of the finger or toe)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phalangem (“phalanx”), from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order, array”). Cf. also the related palanca.
From Latin phalāris, from Ancient Greek φαλαρίς (phalarís).

Borrowed from Latin falcātus (“sickle-shaped, falcate”). First attested in the adjective "sickle-shaped" sense in 1715, and in the noun sense in 1770. The term used in Roman sources is machaera Hispana.

From Latin phalaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “moth; whale”). The semantic shift from "whale" to "moth" occurred in Hellenistic Greek, likely due to an analogy between the fluttering movement of a moth's wings and the fins or spout of a whale. Doublet of balena (“whale”)
Borrowed from Latin fallentia, plural of fallēns.
From falla, of Catalan origin, ultimately from Latin fallere and hence cognate with English fail.
From the past participle of Old Spanish fallir, itself from Latin fallere. Still equivalent to the past participle of modern fallir.
From Old Spanish falsedat, from Latin falsitātem. By surface analysis, falso + -edad.
Inherited from Old Spanish falso, from Latin falsus, with preservation of /alC/ and initial /f/, which Coromines & Pascual suppose is the result of learned pronunciation habits.

parole.significato: A kind of javelin made from a combustible material; a phalarica
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin falārica. First attested in 1490.

Inherited from Old Spanish fama, probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin fāma (partly due to phonetic reasons: initial f did not become h, and because it preserved the Latin sense perfectly; additionally its derivatives are also learned), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bheh₂-mā-, from *bh

parole.significato: family (group of people related to each other)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish familia, a learned borrowing from Latin familia (“slave staff of a household”).
Borrowed from Latin famēlicus (“hungry, famished”). Doublet of jamelgo.

Borrowed from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “image, phantom”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to make visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to cause to appear, bring to light”). Compare Sicilian fantàsimu (“dumb”). Cognate with English phantom.
From Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía, “apparition”).
Borrowed from Latin phantasticus, from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós).

parole.significato: pharisaic (belonging to or characteristic of the Pharisees)

parole.testo: From Latin pharus, from Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros), the Lighthouse of Alexandria.
From faro , from Latin pharus, from Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros).
Borrowed from Latin fascia. Doublet of faja and haz.
Borrowed from Latin fastidiō (“to be disgusted”), from fastidium. Compare the inherited doublet hastiar.
Borrowed from Latin fastīdium. Doublet of hastío.
Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus. Compare the inherited doublet hastioso.
Borrowed from Latin fauce (“(in the) throat”), ablative of faux, much more commonly found in the plural faucēs.
Borrowed from Latin favōnius. Doublet of fagüeño.
From Old Spanish faz, from Latin faciēs. Doublet of facies and haz (“face”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fe, fee, from Latin fidēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”).
Learned borrowing from Latin febrīcula (“light fever”).

parole.significato: date (that which specifies the time when something was made)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish fefaciente, from fe (“faith”) + faciente, from Latin facientem (“making”), the present participle of faciō (“to make”), whose descendant in modern Spanish is hacer. Compare Catalan fefaent.

parole.significato: fellatio (stimulation of the penis with the mouth)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fellātiō, from fellō + -tiō.

parole.significato: feline (of or relating or similar to the cat or the members of zoological family Felidae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fēlīnus (“feline”), from fēlēs (“cat”).
Borrowed from Latin fēlīcem. Compare Catalan feliç.
From Latin fēmina (“woman, female”) + -cida, by analogy with homicida.
From Latin fēmina (“woman, female”) + -cidio, on the pattern of English femicide, by analogy with homicidio.
Inherited from Old Spanish fenir (restructured per various conjugations), from Latin fīnīre. Doublet of finir.
Borrowed from Latin fenestra. Doublet of hiniestra, which was inherited.
From Latin foedus (“hideous”). According to Corominas borrowed from Asturian feu, displacing native hedo. Cognate with Portuguese feio. Compare English fedity.
Inherited from Latin ferīnus. By surface analysis, fiera + -ino.
Learned borrowing from Latin ferōcitātem. By surface analysis, feroz + -idad.
Learned borrowing from Latin ferōx (“wild, untamed”).
From Latin fervēntissimus, superlative of fervēns, ferventis.
Borrowed from Latin ferventem. Doublet of hirviente.
Inherited from Latin fervōrem. Doublet of hervor.

parole.significato: fiber / fibre (a single elongated piece of material)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fibra. Compare the inherited doublet hebra.
Borrowed from Latin fictiōnem. Cognate with English fiction.
Borrowed from Latin fiducia. Compare the obsolete doublet hucia, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”).

Inherited from Old Spanish fiebre, hiebre, probably a semi-learned descendant of Latin febrem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰris, an extension of the root *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn, warm”). Inherited from Old Spanish fiel, from Latin fidēlis.
Inherited from Old Spanish fiera, from Latin fera, from ferus (“wild”, adjective).

Variant of hierro preserving the initial /f/ in Old Spanish fierro, from Latin ferrum.
Semi-learned borrowing of Latin fīxus, perfect passive participle of fīgō (“to fasten, fix”), whence also the inherited doublet hito.

parole.significato: filicide, infanticide (killing of one's own son)
edge, cutting edge (of the blade of an instrument)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish filo, inherited from Latin fīlum. Doublet of hilo. Both were inherited, and it is not entirely clear why the two diverged in pronunciation, with filo coming to mean 'edge' and hilo maintaining the Latin sense of 'string, thread'. Perhaps the /f~h/ variation was exploited t
Borrowed from Latin philologia, from Ancient Greek φιλολογία (philología).
Inherited from Old Spanish filosofar, from Latin philosophārī.
From Old Spanish fin, a semi-learned descendant of Latin fīnis.
From Latin fīnālis. By surface analysis, fin + -al.

parole.significato: to pretend (to act as though something is different from what it is)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fingere. See also the inherited doublet heñir. Cognate with English feign and fiction.
From an alteration of Old Spanish fenir (influenced by fin), from Latin fīnīre. Cf. also the doublet fenecer.
Borrowed from Latin firmāre (“make firm, confirm”). Doublet of hirmar.

parole.significato: fisc; exchequer; national treasury; public treasury

parole.testo: From Latin flaccus, perhaps an early borrowing.
From Latin flagrantem. Doublet of fragante.

parole.significato: to burn, to blaze, to flame
parole.testo: Formed from the root of Latin flamma, with the suffix -ear. Doublet of llamear and flambear.

parole.significato: flatulence, flatus (gas generated in the digestive tract)

parole.testo: From older flueco, from Old Spanish flueco, from Latin floccus (“tuft, wisp of wool”). Regarding the survival of fl- (cf. llama from Latin flamma), compare flaco, flojo, flor.
From Latin phlegmōn, from Ancient Greek φλεγμονή (phlegmonḗ).
Borrowed from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (“to bend, curve”).

parole.significato: inflection (a change in the form of a word that reflects a change in grammatical function)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish floxo (“loose (thing); weak (person)”), inherited form of Latin fluxus. Doublet of flujo. Compare English flux.

Inherited from Old Spanish flor, from Latin flōs (accusative flōrem). The retention of [ɸl] in Old Spanish (instead of a shift to /ʎ/) is unusual and perhaps reflects some form of conservative tendency. Old Spanish /h~ɸ/ became modern /f/ before a glide or liquid (fuego, fiel, fregar, fleco) and aft
Borrowed from Latin Flōra (“Flora (goddess of flowers)”).

parole.significato: flower; floral (of or relating to the flower or flowers)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fluctuātiōnem. Cognate with Galician flutuación.
Borrowed from Latin fluxus. Doublet of flojo, which is inherited.
From Latin flaccidus. Doublet of lacio.
From Latin fluor (“the act of flowing”).

parole.significato: seal (animal belonging to the Pinnipedia parvorder of semi-aquatic marine mammals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish phoca, a learned borrowing from Latin phōca, from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē).
From Latin Phōcaeus, from Ancient Greek Φωκαῖος (Phōkaîos).
Borrowed from Latin focus. Compare the inherited doublet fuego.
Likely from fuego + -ata, ultimately from Latin focus (“hearth”). Compare huérfano (“orphan”) and orfanato (“orphanage”).
Borrowed from Latin folium. Cf. also hoja.

parole.significato: leafy (shaped like a leaf or leaves)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin foliāceus, from folium (“leaf”) (Spanish hoja).
Borrowed from Latin folliculus. Doublet of hollejo, which was inherited.

Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin fundus  PIE word  *bʰudʰmḗn The preservation of the initial older 'f' in this word may be to distinguish it from the doublet hondo, which became an adjective and continued its phonetic evolution as expected. Also the doublet of fundo, a later borrowing.

parole.significato: forensic (relating to the scientific investigation of evidence for a court of law)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fōrma. Compare the inherited doublet horma.
Borrowed from Latin formātiōnem. Cognate with Catalan formació, Occitan formacion.
Borrowed from Latin fornicātor. By surface analysis, fornicar + -ador.
Borrowed from Latin forum. Doublet of fuero.
From Old Spanish forca + -eta, the first element from Latin furca. Doublet of horqueta, if not simply the obsolete version of it. Compare French fourchette.
Borrowed from Latin fortitūdō. Compare the rare semi-learned borrowing fortitúdine and the inherited forcedumbre.
Borrowed from Latin fortūna, from fors (“chance, luck”).
From Latin fūrunculus. Cognate with English furuncle.
Borrowed from Latin fossa. See also huesa, inherited from the same source. Cognate with English fosse (“moat, ditch”).

parole.significato: to dig a hole or moat

From Latin flagrantem. Doublet of flagrante.
From Latin fragrāre, probably a semi-learned borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin fragor (“a breaking to pieces”), from frangere (“to break”).
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Latin fabricāre. Doublet of the borrowing fabricar.

parole.significato: French (as in French food, clothing, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin francēnsis. By surface analysis, Francia (“France”) + -és.
Borrowed from Latin frangere (“to break, shatter”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-. Compare the inherited dialectal (esp. Asturias region) or Old Spanish frañir, frañer.
Inherited from Latin flascō, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ; see also Old High German flasca, Old Norse flaska, English flask. Doublet of fiasco. Cognate with English flask.

parole.significato: brotherly, fraternal (of or characteristic of brothers)
to wash (to clean with a sponge, brush, rag)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish fregar, from Latin fricāre. Compare English fray, Italian fregàre.
Possibly from Latin frēnāre, but more likely derived later in Spanish from freno, and first attested 1591. Cf. also enfrenar and refrenar.

parole.significato: frenzy (state of wild activity or panic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: brake (device used to slow or stop the motion of a wheel or vehicle)

Inherited from Old Spanish fruente, from Latin frōns, frontem.
Inherited from Old Spanish fresno, freisno, frexno, frexeno, Latin fraxinus (“ash tree”), from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”).
Inherited from Old Spanish friir (with dissimilation), from Latin frīgere (with a change in verb class), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

From frío + -dad, possibly influenced by fealdad or alternatively a phonetic evolution of Latin frīgiditātem, through a hypothetical early Ibero-Romance or Proto-Spanish intermediate form *friyeddade.
Inherited from Latin phaseolus, probably from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos).

parole.testo: Irregular past participle of freír (cf. freído), corresponding to Latin frīctus. After -ī-, Latin -ct- regularly corresponds to Spanish -t- (rather than Spanish -ch-).
Inherited from Latin fabrica (“workshop”). Doublet of forja, fábrica, and fragua.
Borrowed from Latin frontispicium. Compare English frontispiece.
Borrowed from Latin frūctificāre. Compare Ladino frochiguar, fruchiguar, Old Spanish fruchiguar.
Borrowed from Latin frūstrātiōnem. Cognate with English frustration.

parole.significato: any fruit from a plant, whether sweet or not (like avocado or tomato), edible or not

Borrowed from Latin framea. First attested in 1598.
Borrowed from Latin frīgidus, from frīgō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sriges-, *sriHges-. Compare the inherited doublet frío. Cognate with English frigid.

Inherited from Latin follem, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolǵʰnis, derivative of *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).
