Inherited from Old Spanish fuero, from Latin forum, from Proto-Italic *forom, from *fworom, from *θworom, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwór-o-, from *dʰwer- + *-os. Doublet of foro.
Inherited from Latin fortem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fort”). Compare English forte ("a strength").

parole.significato: to put to flight, to cause to flee

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fugācem, from fugiō.
Borrowed from Latin fulmināre, from Latin fulmen.
Borrowed from Latin fūmigāre. Compare humear, an inherited doublet.
Learned borrowing from Latin fundātiōnem. By surface analysis, fundar + -ción.

parole.significato: foundation (lowest and supporting part or member of a wall)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish fundir, a learned borrowing from Latin fundō. Doublet of hundir (“to sink”). Cognate with English found (“to melt”) and fuse.
Borrowed from Latin fundus. Doublet of fondo.
From Latin fungī (“to perform”). Cognate with fungible.

parole.significato: to act as, to serve in a position

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fūrtīvus (“stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft”), from fūr (“thief”).

Inherited from Latin fūstis (“stick, club”). Noting the unexpected /f-/, Coromines & Pascual dismiss the possibility of a borrowing from neighbouring Romance varieties (cf. Galician fuste) and point out that the word was common in medieval times but restricted to more technical registers afterwards,
Borrowed from Latin fabrica (“workshop”). Doublet of forja, fragua, and froga.
Borrowed from Latin fābula. Doublet of the inherited habla.
Borrowed from Latin facilis. Compare English facile.
Borrowed from Latin pharmacum, from Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon).
Borrowed from Latin farrāgō (“mixed fodder; mixture, hodgepodge”). Compare the inherited doublets herrén and regional rain.
Borrowed from Latin faecula, diminutive of faex (“residue, dregs”).
Borrowed from Latin fēmina. Doublet of hembra, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix, “purple, crimson, phoenix”).
Learned borrowing from Latin feretrum, from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron).
Borrowed from Latin ferreus (“made of iron; hard; rigid”).
Borrowed from Latin fertilis (“fruitful, fertile”), from ferō (“to bear, to carry”).
Borrowed from Latin ferula. Compare obsolete English ferula.
Borrowed from Latin fībula (“buckle”). Compare the inherited doublet hebilla.
From Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth, nature, quality”), from φύω (phúō, “to grow”).

parole.significato: fornix (bundle of fibres at the base of the brain)
fovea (the retinal fovea, or fovea centralis, responsible for sharp central vision)
parole.testo: From Latin fovea (“ditch, pit”). Doublet of hoya.
Borrowed from Latin fulica. Doublet of focha and foja.

parole.significato: Gaditanian (of, from or relating to Cádiz)

parole.testo: From Latin galaxiās, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “milky”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).
Borrowed from Latin Galīlaeus, from Ancient Greek Γᾰλῑλαῖος (Gălīlaîos), from Ancient Greek Γᾰλῑλαίᾱ (Gălīlaíā, “Galilee”).
Inherited from Latin Gallaecus. Compare Galician galego and Portuguese galego.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin gallīna.
From Latin gallīnācea, femine of gallīnāceus. Compare Romanian găinaț.
Inherited from Latin gallīnāceus. Compare the borrowed doublet gallináceo.
Inherited from Latin gallīnārium, from gallīna. Compare Portuguese galinheiro, Italian gallinaio.
Inherited from Latin gallīnārius. Equivalent to gallina + -ero.
Borrowed from Latin gallīnāceus. Compare the inherited doublet gallinazo.
Inherited from Latin gallus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-.
From gallofo (“loafing”) + -ear, from gallofa (“food given to beggars”), from the Latin Gallī offa (literally “Frenchman's food, food given to Frenchmen”).
Learned borrowing from Latin galacticus, from Ancient Greek γαλακτικός (galaktikós, “milky”).
Borrowed from Latin ganglion, from Ancient Greek [Term?].
Inherited from Old Spanish grafio, garfio by metathesis, from Latin graphium.
Past participle of Old Spanish garrir (“to chat, prattle”), from Latin garrīre (“to chatter”).

parole.significato: Of a parrot or parakeet, to make its characteristic cry

parole.testo: From gas (“gas”) and Latin ductus (“conducting”); formed according to the model of oleoducto (“oil pipeline”).
Likely inherited from Latin vastāre, with the initial consonant influenced by Frankish *wōstijan and with the resulting /ɡw/ reducing to /g/ in unstressed initial position, as also in galardón.
Partly Latin vastāre, partly from a Germanic language (compare English waste). Cognate with Portuguese gasto.

parole.significato: Stupid and bad-mannered rural man from the Spanish countryside; yokel, hick
parole.testo: Unknown, with mainly two Germanic and Arabic etymologies considered. The traditional early proposition was a descent from Latin ganeō (“glutton, libertine”), but this has been mostly discarded. Borrowed from Latin gemma (“bud, precious stone, jewel”). Doublet of yema. According to Coromines and Pascual, a recent learned borrowing not registered even in the 18th-century first edition of the DRAE (Diccionario de Autoridades).

Borrowed from Latin gemellus, from geminus (“twin, paired”), (compare French jumeau, Italian gemello, Portuguese gêmeo, Romanian geamăn). Compare mellizo, melgo, mielgo, inherited from related roots. Compare English gimbal.
Semi-learned modification (based on the original Latin etymology) and conjugation change of Old Spanish emer, itself inherited from Latin gemere. Compare Portuguese gemer.

parole.significato: a generalization, a generality, an unspecific or vague statement
to generate, to create, to produce, to cause

parole.testo: From Latin generātus + -ivo, from Latin generō.
Borrowed from Latin geniālis (“of or relating to marriage; festive, genial”), from genius (“guardian spirit”) + -ālis.
Borrowed from Latin genius, related to gignō (“to beget”) and genus (“birth, origin”).
Latinizing modification of Old Spanish yente, inherited from Latin gentem.
Borrowed from Latin gentīlis, from gēns (“Roman clan”).
Borrowed from Latin gentīlicius, from Latin gentīlis, whence English gentile.
From Latin geōdes, from Ancient Greek γεώδης (geṓdēs, “earthy”).
From Latin geometria, from Ancient Greek.
From Latin germānus (“brother”) + -ía. Doublet of hermano.
From Latin gestus, whence English gesture.
From Latin Geta, from Ancient Greek Γέτης (Gétēs).
From Latin geogrăphus, from Ancient Greek γεωγράφος (geōgráphos), equivalent to geo- + -grafo.
Learned borrowing from Latin geōmētrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs).
From Latin gibba. Compare English gibbous.
Learned borrowing from Latin gigās, from Ancient Greek γίγᾱς (gígās, “giant”). See also English giant.

parole.significato: gym, gymnasium (a room or building equipped for indoor sports)
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion). Compare Catalan gimnàs, French gymnase, Italian ginnasio, Portuguese ginásio, English gymnasium.
Learned borrowing from Latin gynaecēum, from Ancient Greek γυναικεῖον (gunaikeîon).

From Latin gȳrāre, from Latin gȳrus (“circle”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros). Doublet of yirar. Compare with French gyrer, Galician xirar, Portuguese girar, Italian girare. Compare also English gyrate, English gyro.
Borrowed from Latin glandem. Compare the inherited doublet lande or llande, now mostly regional/dialectal terms. Cf. also landre.
Borrowed from Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”).
Inherited from Old Spanish gloria, borrowed from Latin glōria.
From Latin glōssārium (“glossary”), from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).
From Latin gluttō, from gluttiō (“to swallow”).
Borrowed from Latin globulus. Cognate with English globule.

Inherited from Old Spanish gouernaçion, governaçion, from Latin gubernātiōnem (“direction, management, government”), or based on Old Spanish gouernar (“to govern”). Analytically from gobernar (“to govern”) + -ción.
Inherited from Old Spanish gouernador, from Latin gubernātōrem (“director, governor”), from gubernō (“to direct, manage, govern”).
Inherited from Old Spanish gobernar, gouernar, from Latin gubernāre, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer”).
From Latin gōbius; see English goby.
Inherited from Latin Gothus, from Proto-Germanic *gutô. The Latin American sense Spaniard is rooted in the legendary Gothic origin of many Iberian noble families.
Inherited from Old Spanish gola, from Latin gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- (“throat”). Doublet of the borrowing gula.

From Latin delphīnus, influenced by golfo. See also delfín.
Inherited from Old Spanish golondrina, from Latin hirundinem, with metathesis. Compare Portuguese andorinha.
Inherited from Old Spanish gordo, from Latin gurdus. Compare English gravity.

They also acknowledge the possibility that gorgojo was simply inhe
From Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ), from γοργός (gorgós, “terrible”).

parole.significato: a drop or small amount of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish gota, from Latin gutta. Compare English gout.
Inherited from Old Spanish gozo, from Latin gaudium.

Borrowed from Latin grātiōsus, from grātia. Compare English gracious.

parole.significato: a sieve used to shred and flatten soil already ploughed
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cratis. Compare Portuguese grade, Italian grata. First attested ca. 1490 in Alonso Fernández de Palencia's Universal vocabulario en latín y romance.

parole.significato: gradient (the rate at which a physical quantity increases or decreases relative to change in a given variable, especial…

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish grado (“staircase; rank, dignity”), inherited from Latin gradus (“a step, pace; step of a staircase; degree”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”). Inherited from Latin grāmĭna, plural of grāmen. Compare Portuguese grama.

parole.significato: grammar; grammatical (of or relating to grammar)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish grammático, borrowed from Latin grammaticus.

parole.significato: a grass, a gramineous plant (plant of the family Poaceae)

Inherited from Latin (mālum) granātum (literally “apple with many seeds”).
Inherited from Old Spanish grande, from Latin grandem (“large; great”), ultimately of unknown origin. Cognate with English grand and Ladino grande.

Borrowed from Latin grandiloquus, from grandis (“great, full”) + to loquor (“speak”).

Inherited from Latin grunnīre, probably ultimately imitative. Compare Portuguese grunhir, French grogner, Danish grynte, Old High German grunnizon, German grunzen.

Borrowed from Latin graphicus (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, “belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ-.
Learned borrowing from Latin gravidus, from gravis (“heavy”).

Borrowed from Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form gosto. The learned word has a more abstract meaning overall.
From Latin gelidus (“cold”), from gelū (“frost; chill”).
Learned borrowing from Latin genus (through a regularized accusative *generum).
Borrowed from Latin genesis, from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis).

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish faba, from Latin faba, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”). Cognate with English fava.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin habeas corpus ad subjiciendum (“You (shall) have the body to be subjected to (examination)”), see above for more details.

parole.significato: to have; forms the perfect aspect
parole.testo: Latinised respelling of Old Spanish aver, from Latin habēre, habeō (“have, hold”), probably from Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”). Cognate with French avoir, Italian avere, Occitan aver, Portuguese haver, Romanian avea, avere, and Sardini
From Latin habilitātem. Cognate with English ability.

parole.significato: to enable (to give strength or ability to)

From habitar + -dor, or possibly a borrowing from Latin habitātor.

parole.significato: to inhabit, to live or dwell in / on
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin habitāre. Cognate with English habit (“to clothe”) (v.).
Inherited from Old Spanish fabla, from Latin fābula (“discourse”). Compare fábula, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Latin fābulāntem. By surface analysis, hablar (“to speak”) + -ante.

parole.significato: to talk; to speak; to communicate using words
parole.testo: From Old Spanish fablar, from Latin fābulārī (“chat, converse”). Doublet of fabular, which was borrowed from Latin.

Inherited from Old Spanish fazer, from Latin facere. From harina + -ero or from Latin farīnārius. Cf. also harnero.

parole.significato: to bore, tire, to make fed up

parole.testo: From Latin fartus (“stuffed”), from Latin farciō whence English farce. For sense evolution compare English fed up. Cognate with Galician farto, Portuguese farto, Asturian fartu and Catalan fart.
From hastío + -oso, or from Latin fastīdiōsus, and thus a doublet of the borrowed fastidioso.
Inherited from Latin fastīdium. Doublet of fastidio.
Inherited from Old Spanish faya, from Latin [materia] fāgea, from fāgus, from Proto-Italic *fāgos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos. Compare Galician and Portuguese faia.
Inherited from Latin fascis (“bundle”). Cognate with English fagot (“bundle of sticks, twigs or branches”). Doublet of fajo and feje.
Inherited from Old Spanish faz, from Latin faciēs. Doublet of facies and faz.
Inherited from Latin fascia (“band, strip, swathe”).
Borrowed from Latin hebdomada (“week”), from hebdomas (“seven, week”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “the number seven”), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”).
Inherited from Latin fibra. Compare the borrowed doublet fibra.
Borrowed from Latin hebraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī́).

Inherited from Old Spanish fechizo, from Latin factīcius (“artificial”, adjective), from factus (“made”) + -īcius. Compare the borrowed doublet facticio. Compare English factitious. Cognate with Portuguese feitiço.

Inherited from Old Spanish felecho, from Latin filictum (“fernbrake”), from filix (“fern”). Compare Asturian felechu, Friulian felet, Galician fieito, and Portuguese feto.
From Latin heliacus, from Ancient Greek ἡλιακός (hēliakós).

Inherited from Old Spanish femna, fembra, from Latin fēmina (“female”), from Proto-Italic *fēmanā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(f.) one who is sucked; one who suckles”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”). Doublet of fémina, which is a direct borrowing.

parole.significato: hemina (a Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L)

From Latin hēmisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).
Borrowed from Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “violent bleeding”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break asunder, to tear, to shatter”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fender, from Latin findere, findō, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).
Inherited from Latin fēnum, early monophthongized variant of faenum, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-. Compare English fennel and fenugreek.

Inherited from Old Spanish heredad, from Latin hērēditātem.
Inherited from Old Spanish heredero, from Latin hērēditārius, from hēres (“heir”).
Borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”).

Inherited from Old Spanish herencia, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin haerentia, an irregular derivation from Latin hēres. The inherited Old Spanish herença didn't survive into modern Spanish. Compare Ladino erensya, Portuguese herança, Galician herdanza.

From herrar (“to horseshoe”), from hierro (“iron”), from Latin ferrum (“iron”).

Inherited from Old Spanish ferrén, ferraine, from Latin farrāgō via a Vulgar Latin form *ferrāgō, ferrāginem.

Inherited from Old Spanish fervir, from Latin fervēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“be hot, boil”). The change in verb class could be by analogy with servir and vivir. Cognate with English brew.
From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon).
Inherited from Old Spanish *fennir, from Latin fingere. See also the borrowed doublet fingir.

Borrowed from Latin hydrophobia, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβία (hudrophobía), equivalent to hidro- + -fobia.
Borrowed from Latin hydraulicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”) + -ικός (-ikós).
Inherited from Latin hedera, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to seize, grasp, take”).
From earlier yelo, from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). Compare English gel.

parole.significato: grass (plant of the family Poaceae or plant that resembles grasses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish yerva, from Latin herba. Compare Catalan herba, Portuguese erva.

Inherited from Old Spanish fierro, from Latin ferrum. Doublet of fierro (“branding iron”, inherited from Latin) and ferro (“anchor of a galley”, probably borrowed from Catalan). Other Romance cognates include French fer, Italian ferro, Portuguese ferro, and Romanian fier.

Borrowed from Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”).
Inherited from Old Spanish figo, from Latin fīcus (“fig, fig tree”). Cognate with English fig.
Inherited from Old Spanish figuera, from Latin fīcāria, from fīcus (“fig”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fija, from Latin fīlia.
Inherited from Old Spanish fijo, from Latin fīlius.
From Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).
Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos, “song, hymn”).

parole.significato: to inflate or fill with air or liquid
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish finchar, from Latin īnflāre (“to inflate something, blow into it”). The phonetic development involved consonant spread of the medial [f], namely via *hinhláɾe or *finfláɾe, cf. hallar, and see also henchir. Doublet of borrowed inflar. Cognate with English inflate, Portugue

From hinchar + -zón (found in Old Spanish as finchazón), possibly corresponding to Latin īnflātiōnem, and therefore a doublet of inflación. Compare Portuguese inchação, Italian enfiagione, dialectal French enflaison, archaic Romanian umflăciune.
Inherited from Latin genesta. Doublet of genista.
Borrowed from Latin hypocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston), from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “underneath”) + καίειν (kaíein, “to light a fire, burn”).
From Latin hypotheca, from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē). Compare Scottish English hypothec.
From Scientific Latin hypoxia, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-), English oxygen and -ia.
From Latin hyperbaton, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβατόν (huperbatón, “overstepping”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go, move, walk”).
From Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of hipérbola.
Borrowed from Latin hippodromos, from Ancient Greek ἱππόδρομος (hippódromos), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + δρόμος (drómos, “course”).
Inherited from Latin ferventem. Doublet of ferviente.
Borrowed from Latin hȳsōpum, hyssōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), from some Semitic source. See the Greek term for more information. Cognate with English hyssop.
Borrowed from Latin Hispalēnsis, from Hispalis (“Seville”) + -ēnsis (“-ese”), equivalent to Spanish + -ense.
Borrowed from Latin Hispānus, from Hispānia + -ānus.
Borrowed from Latin hispanicus, from Hispānia.
Borrowed from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).
From Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). See histeria.

parole.significato: Traditional New Mexican Spanish variant of hijo.
parole.testo: From the diminutive of hijo (hijito), with apheresis, from Old Spanish fijo, from Latin fīlius (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Spelled as hito, rather than the expected jito, due to confluence of English and Spanis

parole.significato: from or relative to today, nowaday, current, present, present-day

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hōc annō, ablative of hic + annus (“this year”). Compare Portuguese ogano and Asturian anguaño.
From hojalde, from Latin foliātilis (panis) (literally “bread of leaves”).

Inherited from Old Spanish omne, from Latin hominem, homō, from Old Latin hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ (“earthling”). The Old Spanish form omne was first dissimilated to omre and then a gliding sound -b- arose before the -r-. Compare the same development in cumbre, hembra, nombre, hambre, co
Inherited from Old Spanish ombro, from Latin humerus, umerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”). Doublet of húmero.
Inherited from Old Spanish omicidio, omizidio, homicidio, homizidio, homiçidio, omeçidio, borrowed from Latin homicīdium. It replaced the inherited variant omezillo, omecillo in Old Spanish.
Borrowed from Latin homologāre, equivalent to homólogo + -ar.
Inherited from Old Spanish fonda, from Latin funda.

Inherited from Old Spanish fondo, from Latin fundus, with the Latin noun taking on an adjectival sense in Spanish.  PIE word  *bʰudʰmḗn An alternative theory sees the Old Spanish fondo as a shortening of an earlier, pre-literary *perfondo, from the Latin adjective profundus instead, which matches wi
Inherited from Old Spanish onestat, from Latin honestatem.

Inherited from Old Spanish onestat, onestad, from Latin honestātem. The ending was altered to conform to the common suffix -idad; according to Coromines and Pascual, first attested in this new form in the 15th century, in a work of Alfonso de Palencia.
Borrowed from Latin honestus, an adjective based on honor.
Inherited from Old Spanish onor, from Latin honōrem.
Borrowed from Latin honōrābilis. Equivalent to honor + -able.
Borrowed from Latin honorāre. Compare the inherited honrar.
Inherited from Old Spanish onrra, onra, derived from onrrar + -a, the former from Latin honōrāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish hondrado, from Latin honorātus.
Inherited from Old Spanish hondrar, onrrar, onrar, from Latin honōrāre. Doublet of honorar, which was borrowed.
Borrowed from Latin hoplītēs m, from Ancient Greek ὁπλῑ́της (hoplī́tēs, “hoplite”).

parole.significato: hour (a time period of sixty minutes)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Horātiānus, from Horātius.

parole.significato: a hole or other perforation that crosses something from side to side, or that crosses all of its parts
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin forātum < forātus (“drilled, pierced”), perfect passive participle of forō.
Inherited from Old Spanish forca, from Latin furca.
Borrowed from Latin horizontem, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn).
Inherited from Latin fōrma. Compare the borrowed doublet forma.
Inherited from Old Spanish formiga, from Latin formīca.
From horno + -ear, from Old Spanish forno, from Latin furnus.
Inherited from Old Spanish forno, from Latin furnus.

Borrowed from Latin horrorem. Cf. also the popular Old Spanish horrura, inherited from a derivative of the Latin or with a change of suffix, and taking on the meaning of "dirtiness, filth, impurity, scum"; comparable to derivatives of horridus in other Romance languages, like Italian ordo, Old Frenc

parole.significato: horticulture (art or science of cultivating gardens)

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin fuscus (compare Portuguese fosco, fusco, Italian fosco, Catalan fosc, Old French fusque).
Borrowed from Latin hospitium, from hospes (“host, guest”).
Borrowed from Latin hospitalitātem, from hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“host, guest”).
Inherited from Old Spanish oy, from Latin hodiē. Cognate with Portuguese hoje, and Italian oggi.
Inherited from Latin fovea. Doublet of fóvea.
Inherited from Latin fovea, with a change in gender or possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *foveum. Compare Portuguese fojo, Galician foxo, Asturian fueyu.
Inherited from Old Spanish foz, from Latin falcem.
Inherited from Old Spanish foç, from Latin fōcem, early monophthongized variant of faucem.

parole.significato: acre; as much land as can be ploughed in a day
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish huebra, from Latin opera. See also obra, which was influenced by the verb obrar. Also a doublet of ópera, a borrowing from Italian.
Derived from an Old Spanish verb ocar or aocar, from the Latin occāre (“to harrow”) (whence also Portuguese oco), from Latin occa. Related to German Egge.
Inherited from Old Spanish huerco (“Hell; the Devil”), from Latin Orcus (“the underworld; the god Pluto”). Cognate with English ogre and orc. Doublet of orco and ogro.
Inherited from Latin hortus. Cognate with Ladino guerta.
Inherited from Latin hortus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰortós.
Inherited from Latin fossa. See also fosa, borrowed from the same source.

Inherited from Old Spanish huesso, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan os, French os, Interlingua osso, Italian osso, Portuguese osso, Romanian os, Sardinian ossu. Political sense comes

Inherited from Latin hostem (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostim, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstim (“guest, stranger”). Compare Catalan host (“army”), Italian oste (“army, host”), Romanian oaste (“army, host”).
From Latin hūmānus, from homō (“human being”).
Inherited from Latin fūmāre. Doublet of fumar.
First attested in 1498. Borrowed from Latin humectans, equivalent to humectar + -ante.
Inherited from Old Spanish umildat, from Latin humilitātem. Equivalent to humilde + -dad.
Modified (after humildad) from Old Spanish humil, borrowed from Latin humilis.
Inherited from Old Spanish fumo, from Latin fūmus. Doublet of fumo. Compare Ladino umo.
Borrowed from Latin hūmōrem. Cognate with English humor.
Inherited from Old Spanish fundir. Doublet of fundir (“to cast, melt”), from Latin fundere. Compare English found (“to cast metal”), founder (“to sink”).
From huro, ultimately from Latin forō. Compare Portuguese buraco, Galician buraco, furaco, Asturian buracu, furacu.
Inherited from Old Spanish furto. Cognate with English furtive.
Inherited from Latin fūsus. Cognate with English fuse.

Inherited from Old Spanish huésped, from Latin hospitem, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European root *gʰóstipotis, a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. Doublet of host. See also hueste.
From Latin habilis (“suitable, skillful”). Cognate with English able.
Borrowed from Latin helīcem, from Ancient Greek ἕλῑξ (hélīx, “spiral”).
Borrowed from Latin hērōem, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs).
From Latin hibridus, hybridus (“hybrid”, adjective), from hibrida f (“hybrid”, noun), most likely from Ancient Greek, with influence from ὕβρις (húbris).

Inherited from Old Spanish orrio, from Latin horreum, from Ancient Greek ὡρεῖον (hōreîon). The standard form in modern Spanish, with /e/ rather than /j/, appears to be the result of a latinizing modification. Compare Asturian horriu, horru and Catalan orri.
Borrowed from Latin hūmidus, variant of ūmidus.
Borrowed from Latin humerus. Doublet of hombro.

parole.significato: The ninth letter of the Spanish alphabet, written in the Latin script.
unadapted form of ibídem (“ibidem”) (in the same place)

parole.testo: From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian hbj.

parole.significato: Iberian (of, from or relating to Iberia)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Hibēricus (“Iberian”). First attested in late 16th century.
Learned borrowing from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”). Compare Portuguese ideia.

Pseudo-Latinism, derived from idem (“same”) + potentia (“the quality of having power”), coined as a calque of English idempotence, equivalent to ídem + potencia. Cognate with Catalan idempotència, French idempotence, Italian idempotenza, Portuguese idempotência, and Romanian idempotență.
From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “shape, form”).
Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).
Learned borrowing from Latin īdōlatrīa, haplological form of īdōlolatrīa.
Borrowed from Latin idōneitātem. Cognate with English idoneity.
Learned borrowing from Latin īdōlatra, haplological form of īdōlolatra.
Borrowed from Latin idōneus. Cognate with English idoneous.
Inherited from Old Spanish ignorançia, ynorançia (early 13th c.), a learned borrowing from Latin ignōrantia. Doublet of añoranza.
From Latin īgnōrante or īgnōrantī, singular ablative of īgnōrāns (“ignorant”).

parole.significato: to not know, be ignorant of
parole.testo: From Old Spanish ignorar, a learned borrowing from Latin ignōrāre. Doublet of añorar.
Inherited from Old Spanish igual~egual (both common in the 13th century), from Latin aequālis. Cognate with English equal.
Inherited from Latin aequālitātem, from aequālis (“equal, even”). By surface analysis, igual + -dad. Compare Catalan igualtat, French égalité, Portuguese igualdade.
From i- + legítimo, or borrowed from Latin illēgitimus.
From Latin Ilergetes. Probably related to Iberian Iltirta and Latin Ilerda.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Elche
parole.testo: Derived from Latin Illicitānus, from Illici.
From assumed singular of Latin Īlōtae (attested only in the plural), from Ancient Greek Εἱλώται (Heilṓtai), plural of Εἱλώτης (Heilṓtēs, “helot”).
Borrowed from Latin illūmināre. Doublet of alumbrar.
From Latin imāginātiōnem, from imāgō (“appearance, likeness”).
From Latin imāginārī, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

parole.significato: dumb, having the properties of an imbecile
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin imbēcillus, from in- (“no”) + baculum (“walking stick, staff”), in the sense of “weak, vulnerable”.
From Latin imitātiōnem. Cognate with English imitation.
From Latin imitātor. Cognate with English imitator.

parole.significato: to imitate, to mimic, to ape, to copy, to copycat, to impersonate, to simulate
parole.testo: From Latin imitārī. Cognate with English imitate.
From Latin impatientem; equivalent to im- + paciente.
From Latin impassibilis, from passibilis. Compare English impassible.
Borrowed from Latin impedīre. Cf. the related empecer.
Borrowed from Latin impellere. Compare the inherited doublet empeller.
Borrowed from Latin imperāre (“command, govern”); Cf. the dialectal emprar and semi-learned Old Spanish emperar.
From Latin imperfectus. By surface analysis, in- + perfecto.

Borrowed from Latin imperiālis (“of the empire or emperor, imperial”), from imperium (“empire, imperial government”) + -ālis, from imperō (“command, order”), from im- (“form of in”) + parō (“prepare, arrange; intend”).
From Latin impermeābilis, equivalent to im- + permeable.
From im- + plantar or Latin implantāre.
From Latin implēre, with influence from inflāre
Borrowed from Latin implicāre. Doublet of emplear.
Borrowed from Latin impōnere. By surface analysis, in- + poner.

parole.significato: to matter, to be important [with a ‘someone’] (often translated idiomatically with English care or mind, with subject a…
to impregnate, permeate (to fill pores or spaces with a substance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin impraegnāre. Doublet of empreñar.
Learned borrowing from Latin improvīsus. Equivalent to in- + pro- + viso.
Borrowed from Latin imprūdentia. Cognate with English imprudence.
Borrowed from Latin imprūdentem. By surface analysis, in- + prudente. Cognate with English imprudent.
Borrowed from Latin impulsiōnem. Cf. empujón, which may be a doublet.

parole.significato: to impute; to ascribe; to attribute

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin impetīgō. Doublet of empeine.
Borrowed from Latin in mediās rēs (literally “into the middle of things”).
From Latin inaccessibilĭtātem, equivalent to in- + accesibilidad.
Learned borrowing from Latin inaugurāre (“approve on the basis of omens”).
From Latin incapācitātem; in- + capacidad. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese incapacidade.
From Latin incapax. By surface analysis, in- + capaz.
Borrowed from Latin incidentem, present participle of incidō (“to fall, to occur”).

parole.significato: to have influence or affect on, to have bearing on

parole.testo: From Latin incisus, from incidĕre (“to cut (brief)”).

parole.significato: to incite, to provoke, to egg on
to include, to enclose, to contain

parole.testo: From Latin incohatus. Cognate with English inchoation.
Borrowed from Latin incohāre (“to begin”), cognate with English inchoate.

parole.significato: not capable of catching fire and burning; not flammable
to bother; to annoy; to vex

parole.testo: From Latin incommoditātem; By surface analysis, in- + comodidad.
Borrowed from Latin incommunicabĭlis, equivalent to in- + comunicable.
Borrowed from Latin inconscientia, equivalent to in- + consciencia.

parole.significato: incorporeal (having no material form or physical substance)

parole.testo: From Latin incruentus. By surface analysis, in- + cruento.
Borrowed from Latin incubāre (“to lie on”).

parole.significato: to instill, inculcate (in), drum (review to establish memorization)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incultus. By surface analysis, in- + culto.

parole.significato: incognito, anonymous, unknown (with a hidden or unknown identity)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin incolumem, from incolumis (“unimpaired, safe”).
From Latin indāgātiōnem. By surface analysis, indagar + -ción.
Borrowed from Latin indāgāre (“to follow a trail, to search for”).
Learned borrowing from Latin indigentia (“need, demand”).
Learned borrowing from Latin indigentem (“needing, requiring”).
Borrowed from Latin indīgestus (“confused, disordered”) (in Late Latin also "suffering from indigestion").
Borrowed from Latin indignātiōnem. Cognate with English indignation.
Borrowed from Latin indignārī (“to be indignant”).
From Latin indolentem, accusative singular masculine and feminine of indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“pain”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ineffābilis (“ineffable, inexpressible”), from in- (“not”) + effābilis (“utterable”).

parole.significato: inertia (the property of a body that resists change to its uniform motion)
inevitable, inescapable, unavoidable (unable to be avoided)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inexcusabilis. By surface analysis, in- + excusable.
Borrowed from Latin infacundus. By surface analysis, in- + facundo.

parole.significato: childhood (period of human development from birth until puberty)

parole.testo: From an alteration of Old Spanish ifante, from Latin īnfāns, īnfāntem.
From Latin īnfartus. Cognate with English infarct.

parole.significato: to infect (to bring into contact with a substance that causes illness)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin īnferre (“to carry in”).

parole.significato: hell; infernal (of or relating to hell)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish infierno, from Latin īnfernum.
Borrowed from Latin īnfixus, perfect passive participle of infigō (“to fasten, fix, implant”).
Borrowed from Latin īnflātiōnem, equivalent to inflar + -ción. Compare also hinchazón, which may be a doublet.
Borrowed from Latin īnflāre. Compare the inherited doublet hinchar.

parole.significato: inflection (a turning away from a straight course)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnfluere (“to flow in, to invade, to penetrate”).
Borrowed from Latin īnflūxus, from īnfluō.
Borrowed from Latin īnfōrmātiōnem (“formation, conception; education”), from the participle stem of īnformāre (“to inform”).
From Latin īnfractiōnem, from in- + frangere.
From ingenio (“wit”) + -ar, from Latin ingenium. Akin to Italian ingegnarsi.

parole.significato: genius, wit, ingeniousness (faculty to reason and invent quickly)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ingenium. Doublet of engeño.
Learned borrowing from Latin ingerō (“to carry in”). Cognate with English ingest.
Inherited from Latin inguinem. Cognate with English inguen.

parole.significato: ingredient (one of the substances present in a mixture, especially food)
parole.testo: From Latin ingredientem (“entering”), from ingredior (“to enter”).

parole.significato: to join a group, institution, organization, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin ingressus (+ -ar), from in- + gressus; cognate with English ingress.
Borrowed from Latin initiāre. Cf. also comenzar.
Borrowed from Latin inīquus, from in- (“not”) + aequus (“even, plain, flat”).
Borrowed from Latin inīquitātem (“inequality, unevenness”), from inīquus (“uneven, unequal”).
From Latin īnserĕre. Doublet of injertar and insertar

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin īnsertāre (“to insert, to introduce in”), frequentative of īnserō (“to put in, to insert”) (preterite īnseruī, supine īnsertum). Present meaning developed by confusion of the above base verb with the homonymous verb īnserō (“to plant, to graft”) (preterite īnsēvī, s

Deverbal from injertar or semi-learned borrowing from Latin īnsertus (literally “inserted”), later "grafted" by confusion between homonymous īnserō (“to insert”) (perfect passive participle īnsertus) and īnserō (“to graft”) (perfect passive participle īnsitus). Compare also enjerto and inserto, from
From in- + justo, or borrowed from Latin injūstus.
From Latin immaculātus, from in- (“not”) + maculātus (“stained, spotted; defiled, polluted; dishonoured”).
From Latin immiscēre, with influence of immiscui.
Borrowed from Latin immodestus. By surface analysis, in- + modesto.
From Latin immortālis. By surface analysis, in- + mortal.

parole.significato: motionless, immobile, unmoving, still, stationary, static

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin innātus (“inborn”), perfect active participle of innāscor (“be born in, grow up in”).
From Latin innumerus. By surface analysis, in- + número.
From Latin inodorus, from in + odor.
From Latin inoperantem. By surface analysis, in- + operante.

parole.significato: inopportune (inconvenient or occurring at an inappropriate time)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inquietāre, from inquiētus (“restless”).
Borrowed from Latin inquināre (“to defile, to stain”).
Borrowed from Latin īnscrībere, with conjugation based on escribir.

Borrowed from Latin īnsecta (“insects”) (attested in Pliny only in the plural), a calque of ἔντομα (éntoma, “insects”, literally “dissected”), from their segmented bodies, from εν- (en-) + τόμος (tómos, “slice”); calqued based on īnsectus (“notched, dissected”), perfect passive participle of īnsecō.
Learned borrowing from Latin insectivorus. By surface analysis, Latin insecto + Latin -i + Latin vorō.
From Latin in + sēminō (“to plant, sow”), from sēmen.

parole.significato: insensitivity, callousness, cold-heartedness, insensibility, insensitiveness, numbness
parole.testo: Either from insensible + -idad or from Latin īnsēnsibilitātem

parole.significato: to urge (press someone to do something soon)
parole.testo: From Latin īnstāre (“urge, insist”) whence English instant.

parole.significato: to found, to institute, to establish

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnsufficientem, equivalent to in- + suficiente.

parole.significato: insular (of, pertaining to, being, or resembling an island or islands)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnsulāris. By surface analysis, ínsula + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin īnsulsus (“unsalted”). Doublet of soso.
Borrowed from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). Cognate with Sicilian nzìpitu, English insipid.
From Latin integratiōnis, from integratio. Equivalent to integrar + -ción.

parole.significato: to integrate, to embed, to incorporate, to include
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin integrāre. Doublet of entregar (“to deliver”) and enterar (“to inform; to find out”). Cognate with English integrate.
Borrowed from Latin integritātem (“soundness, integrity”), from integer.
Borrowed from Latin intelligentia, which is from inter- (“between”) + legere (“choose, pick out, read”).
Borrowed from Latin intelligentem, variant of intellegēns. Cognate with English intelligent.

parole.significato: darkest (only used with the femenine noun noche, meaning: night)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intempestus, from Latin intempesta nox (literally “darkest night”).
Borrowed from Latin intendere, from in- + tendō. Doublet of entender.
Borrowed from Latin intēnsus. Cf. entesar, inherited from a derivative of the same word.

parole.significato: to try, to attempt; especially: to strain or put forth effort in so doing

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inter-. Doublet of entre-.
Borrowed from Latin interdicere. Compare the inherited doublet entredecir.
Borrowed from Latin interdictum. Compare the inherited doublet entredicho.
Borrowed from Latin interpōnere. Doublet of entreponer. Cognate with English interpose.
From Latin interpretātiōnem, equivalent to interpretar + -ción.
Learned borrowing from Latin interpretātor. By surface analysis, interpretar + -ador.

parole.significato: interregnum (period of time between the end of a sovereign’s reign and the accession of another sovereign)
an interrogation; a questioning or inquiry
to interrupt, to barge in, to disrupt, to disturb, to intrude, to cut in, to break in, to butt in

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intervenīre (“intervene”). Cf. also the archaic form entrevenir, which may have been inherited.

parole.significato: interest (a fraction of the amount of what was borrowed)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intimitātem, from intimus (“inmost”).

parole.significato: to make a sacrifice in order to please the gods

Learned borrowing from Latin litterātūra (“grammar; philology”), from littera (“letter”).
Borrowed from Latin litigāre. Doublet of lidiar, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin lītorālis. Cognate to English littoral, French littoral.
Formed from the root of Latin lixivia (see lejía), or borrowed from a Medieval Latin lixiviāre

Inherited from Old Spanish llaga, from Latin plāga (“hit, strike”). Cognate with Asturian llaga, Catalan plaga, French plaie, Galician and Portuguese chaga, Italian piaga, Romanian plagă, and more distantly with Ancient Greek πληγή (plēgḗ, “wound”). Doublet of plaga (“plague”).
Inherited from Latin plagāre. Doublet of plagar.
Inherited from Old Spanish llama, from Latin flamma.
Inherited from Old Spanish clamar, from Latin clāmāre (“to cry out”). Doublet of clamar, a borrowing from Latin. Cognate with English claim and clamor.
Inherited from Latin plānus. Compare the borrowed doublets plano and piano. Cognate with Galician chan, Italian piano, and Portuguese chão.
Inherited from Latin clāvis (“key”), from Proto-Italic *klāwis, of ultimately Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of clave. Cognate with English clef.

Inherited from Latin applicāre (“to land, to reach the coast”), due to the strong naval tradition in Iberian peninsula. Compare Portuguese chegar, Asturian allegar, also Romanian pleca (“to leave”), though the latter might be associated with folding up tents and leaving (see Latin plicāre).

Inherited from Old Spanish lleno, lenno, inherited from Latin plēnus, whence also Spanish pleno, which is a borrowed doublet. The Latin word derives from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

Inherited from Old Spanish levar, from Latin levāre. The initial /ʎ/ developed from an earlier /lj/ in root-stressed conjugations such as lieva (< Latin lĕvat), where it resulted from the diphthongization of stressed Latin short ĕ to /je/. Eventually /ʎ-/ spread to the entire verb paradigm by analog
Inherited from Latin plōrāre (“cry out”). Compare English implore.

parole.significato: an enclosed arable land next to a house
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin clausa (“enclosed”). Compare with Galician and Portuguese chousa.
Inherited from Old Spanish lluvia, Latin pluvia.
From lluvia + -oso, or from Latin pluviōsus, from pluvia (“rain”).

parole.significato: neuter definite article used only before nominalized adjectives: the, that which is
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish lo (“the; him; it”). As a masculine pronoun, from Latin illum, the accusative masculine singular of ille (“that, that one”). As an article or impersonal neuter pronoun, from Latin illud, the neuter singular of ille. Compare Portuguese o.
Inherited from Old Spanish loar, laudar, from Latin laudāre. Doublet of laudar, which was probably borrowed from Latin but is also found in Old Spanish.

Inherited from Old Spanish lobo, from Latin lupus. Doublet of lupus (“lupus”, a learned borrowing) and Lope (a proper name from Basque). Cognate with French loup, Italian lupo, Galician and Portuguese lobo, Romanian lup, and distantly English wolf.
Borrowed from Latin lotiōnem, from lavo (“wash”).
Learned borrowing from Latin locus. Doublet of luego.
Inherited from Old Spanish lodo, from Latin lutum.
Inherited from Latin lucrārī. Doublet of lucrar.
Inherited from Latin lucrum. Doublet of lucro, which was borrowed. Compare English lucre.
Inherited from Latin lumbus. Cognate with English loin.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of London, capital of England and the United Kingdom
parole.testo: From Latin Londinēnsis and Latin Londinium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lucanicĭa, from Latin lūcānica, influenced by longus.

parole.significato: long-lived, long-living, that lives for a long time

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin longitūdō (“length, longitude”), from longus (“long”).
From Latin longus. In light of the lack of diphthongization, either borrowed from Latin or through another Romance language; cf. the native doublet luengo.
From Latin longissimus, superlative of longus.
Borrowed from Latin longissimus. Doublet of longuísimo.
Inherited from Old Spanish loor (“praise”), from loar, laudar, from Latin laudāre (“to praise”).

parole.significato: An internet user whose videos' voices are made using the speech synthesis software Loquendo.
parole.testo: From Loquendo + -ero, from Latin loquendus, future passive participle of loquor (“to say, speak, tell”).
Inherited from Old Spanish loriga, from Latin lōrīca (“coat of mail, breastplate”).

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Lugo
a type of old Latin oil lamp

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin luctatōrem (compare Portuguese lutador), corresponding to luchar + -dor.

parole.significato: to fight, to battle, to do battle
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin luctārī. Compare Portuguese lutar, French lutter

parole.significato: pike (any carnivorous freshwater fish of the genus Esox)

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin lūcidus. Compare the borrowed doublet lúcido.

Inherited from Old Spanish luziérnega, from Latin lucerna (“lamp”) + the dialectal suffix -aga, from Paleo-Hispanic. The positioning of stress in the antepenultimate syllable is also due to pre-Roman influence.

parole.significato: to profit, win, gain, opportune, obtain lucre
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lucrārī. Compare the inherited lograr.
Borrowed from Latin lucrum. Compare the inherited logro. Cognate with English lucre.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Logroño
parole.testo: From Latin Lucrōniēnsis, from Lucrōnium, a Medieval form of the name, + -ēnsis (“-ese”). Equivalent to Logroño + -ense.

parole.significato: bright, radiant, dazzling, luminous, giving off light
parole.testo: From Latin lūciferum, possibly borrowed. Doublet of Lucifer.
Unknown. Possibly from Latin lūdere (“to play”).

parole.significato: a compulsive gambler; one who exhibits problem gambling
parole.testo: From ludo + -pata, from Latin lūdus (“game; sport”) and Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

Inherited from Old Spanish luego (“then”), from Latin locō (“in the place of, instead of, for”), ablative of locus, from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”). Doublet of locus. Cognate with English lieu and locus.
Inherited from Old Spanish luengo, from Latin longus. Cognate with English long.
Inherited from Old Spanish lueñe, from Latin longē. Cognate with Portuguese longe.
Borrowed from Latin locum tenentem (“place haver, one who holds a place”). Cognate with English lieutenant and French lieutenant. Morphologically equivalent to lugar (“place”) + teniente (“haver”).
Inherited from Old Spanish luxo, from Latin luxus.
From Latin luxuria (“rankness, luxury”), from luxus (“extravagance, luxury”).
Borrowed from Latin lūxuriōsus. by surface analysis, lujuria + -oso.

From Old Spanish lumbre, lumne, from Latin lūmen (“light source”). First attested in the Cantar de mio Cid. The shift /mn/ > /mbɾ/ is regular and expected: compare hambre and hombre. Cognate with Aragonese llumbre, lumbre, Asturian llume, Catalan llum, Galician and Portuguese lume, Italian lume, and
Borrowed from Latin lumen. Doublet of the inherited lumbre.
Borrowed from Latin lūminōsus. Compare lumbroso, probably an inherited doublet.
Inherited from Old Spanish lunes, from Latin Lūnae dīēs, variant of dīēs Lūnae.
Borrowed from Latin lupus. Doublet of lobo.
From Latin lustrum, denoting a lavatory sacrifice after a quinquennial census, possibly cognate to luō (“to wash, cleanse”).

parole.significato: mourning (feeling or expressing sorrow or regret, especially over someone's death)
parole.testo: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin lūctus, rather than an inheritance. A fully inherited form would be expected to be lucho.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūx. Doublet of the inherited luz.
Inherited from Old Spanish luz, from Latin lūx.
Learned borrowing from Latin lacteus, from lac (“milk”) + -eus.
Inherited from Old Spanish lagrima, lagrema, from Latin lacrima, from Old Latin lacruma, dacrima, dacruma, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru-.
Borrowed from Latin lapidem, from Proto-Italic *lapets, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lep-. Doublet of lápiz and probably laude.
From Latin larix, itself from Ancient Greek λάριξ (lárix).
Borrowed from Latin līmitem (“border”). Doublet of linde.
Borrowed from Latin limpidus. Compare limpio, an inherited doublet. Cognate with English limpid.

parole.significato: line (a straight path through two or more points)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin līnea (“line, thread”), from līnum (“flax”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”). Compare the inherited Old Spanish form liña, still used in archaic modern Spanish. Cognate with Portuguese linha, Galician liña, and Catalan línia and llinya.
From Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), from λύρα (lúra, “lyre”).

Possibly from Latin lūbricus (“slippery, slimy”). Perhaps influenced by lūgubris (“gloomy, mournful”). Doublet of lúbrico. Cognate with Portuguese lôbrego and Asturian llóbregu. An alternative theory derives the term directly from lūgubris, with metathesis; in which case the doublet would be lúgubre
Learned borrowing from Latin lūbricus. Compare lóbrego, probably a doublet.
Learned borrowing from Latin lūcidus. Doublet of the inherited lucio.
Borrowed from Latin lugubris. Cf. also lóbrego.

parole.significato: to macerate (to soften in a liquid)

parole.testo: From macho (“sledgehammer”) + -ar, from Latin marculus (“hammer”), possibly a diminutive of marcus (“hammer”), although the latter is attested late and may be a back-formation from marculus.

parole.motivo_incerta: modificatore <unc> nel legame; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: Two alternative theories are: * From Latin marculus (“hammer”), itself related to the base of malleus. * Variant of mazo (“club”).
From the verb machar (“to grind”), from macho (“mallet”), from Latin marculus (“small hammer”).
Inherited from Old Spanish madexa, from Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa). Cognate to Portuguese madeixa, Italian matassa, Romanian mătase.
Inherited from Old Spanish madera, from Latin māteria (compare French matière, Italian materia, Portuguese madeira), from māter (“source”, literally “mother”). Doublet of materia.
Inherited from Latin mātrem (“mother, matron”), from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Compare English matron.
Inherited from Old Spanish madrueña, from Latin māteria (“wood”) + -ōnea.
Inherited from Latin matūrāre. Cognate with English maturate and mature.
Inherited from Old Spanish maduro, from Latin mātūrus.
Inherited from Old Spanish maesse; cf. maeso, variant of maestro. Often theorized to be a rare vestige of the vocative form of Latin magister.
Syncopic form of maestro, from Latin magistrum (“master”).
Inherited from Latin magistrālis (“pertaining to a teacher or master”). Doublet of magistral and mistral.

Inherited from Old Spanish maestre, from Latin magister (“leader, guide”). Coromines and Pascual consider various ways that the word could have made it through: * as a borrowing from Old Catalan or Old Occitan maestre * as an inherited form of the Latin vocative magister * as an inherited form of th
Inherited from Latin magistrum. Doublet of magíster, borrowed from Latin, and máster, borrowed from English.
Borrowed from Latin magistrālis, itself from magister. Doublet of maestral and mistral.
From Latin magnes or Ancient Greek μᾰ́γνης (mắgnēs).
Borrowed from Latin magnus (“big, large”), from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, from *méǵh₂s (“great”). Doublet of maño.
Borrowed from Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”).
Borrowed from Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos). Cf. also mego.
Inherited from Latin macrum, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Cognate with English meager /meagre.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin maculāre, with influence from abollar.

parole.significato: magister (the possessor of a master's degree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin magister. Compare the inherited doublet maestro and maeso, and the English borrowing máster.
Verb based on Old Spanish majo, from Latin malleus. Compare English maul, Galician mallar and Asturian mayar.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of Málaga, Andalusia, Spain

parole.testo: From Latin maledīcere (“to slander, curse”), possibly taken a semi-learned term; cf. By surface analysis, mal + decir.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin maledictiōnem (“evil-speaking, curse”), from maledīcō (“to speak ill of”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin maledictus. Cognate with Asturian and Leonese malditu, Catalan maleït, French maudit, Italian maledetto. Doublet of Old Spanish maldicho.
Borrowed from Latin maledīcentia (“speaking badly of”), from maledīcō (“to speak badly of”).
Inherited from Latin malitia. Doublet of malicia.

parole.significato: a crime, especially against one's liege lord in the medieval period
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish malfeitoría, from Latin malefactor.
Inherited from Old Spanish mal(o) + grado, which stems from Latin grātum (see grātus (“pleasing, acceptable, agreeable, welcome”)).
Borrowed from Latin malitia. Compare the inherited doublet maleza.
Inherited from Old Spanish malo, from Latin malus. Cognate with Ladino malo, Italian malo, Galician mao, Portuguese mau.
Inherited from Latin malva, of Semitic origin.
Borrowed from Latin maleficus, from male (“badly, evilly”) + faciō (“do”).
Borrowed from Latin malleolus. Doublet of majuelo.
Inherited from Latin mammāre, from mamma (“breast”).

parole.significato: wattle (hanging appendage on a goat's neck)

parole.testo: From Latin mammifer: mamma (“teat”) + fero (“to bear”), equivalent to Latin mamma + -fero.

parole.significato: herd, pack, pride, pod (group of animals)
parole.testo: From mano + -ada, or from Latin manuāta, from manus (“hand”).
From Latin mānāre (“pour or gush forth”).
Inherited from Latin mancus (“maimed, crippled”), from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂n-ko- (“maimed in the hand”), from *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én- (“hand”).

parole.significato: Mancunian (of, from or relating to the city of Manchester, England)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish mandar, from Latin mandāre, present active indicative of mandō (“order, commission”).
Probably borrowed from Latin mandūcāre. Doublet of manjar.
Inherited from Latin manica, cognate with Portuguese manga, French manche.

According to Corominas-Pascual, back-formation from manganilla. Less likely, according to RAE, directly from Latin manganum (“manganel”), which is disputed by Corominas-Pascual on the basis of the stress pattern (if derived from Latin, then *mángana would be expected).

parole.significato: stain (a blemish on one's character or reputation)
parole.testo: From Latin macula; cf. mancha, a doublet.

Inherited from Old Spanish mano, from Latin manus, from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry). Cognate with Galician man and Portugu
From an alteration of Latin manipulus (“maniple, handful”), diminutive of manus (“hand”). Doublet of manípulo. Compare Catalan manyopla.
Inherited from Latin mānsuētūdinem. By surface analysis, manso + -dumbre. Doublet of mansuetud, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin mānsiōnem. See also the doublet mesón.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish manteca, mantega, of uncertain further origin. Possibly from Latin mantica or from Paleo-Hispanic, such as Iberian or Celtiberian. Compare Portuguese manteiga.
Borrowed from Latin mantichōra, from Ancient Greek μαρτιχόρας (martikhóras, “man-eater; tiger”), from Old Persian 𐎶𐎼𐎫𐎡𐎹 (*martiya, “man, human being, mortal”) + 𐎧𐎺𐎠𐎼 (*χvāra, “eater”).

parole.significato: to manumit, to emancipate (to free from slavery)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mania or Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
Inherited from Old Spanish manipulo, maniplo (early 13th c.), from Latin manipulus, diminutive of manus (“hand”). Doublet of manopla.

parole.significato: map (sheet with geographical information on it)
parole.testo: From Latin mappa (“napkin, starting signal in a race”), see map for more.
From Latin mappa (“map”) + mundī (“of the world”).
Borrowed from Latin māchinārī (“scheme, plot”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Morphological doublet of maznar, an inherited form.
Inherited from Old Spanish mar (“sea”), from Latin mare (“sea”), from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. osp + mar. Compare French mer, Italian mare, Portuguese mar, Romanian mare.

parole.significato: strip of terrain in a field marked before sowing.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish marzen, from Latin marginem. Doublet of margen.
Borrowed from Latin mare magnum (literally “great sea”).
From Latin margarīta, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs).

Inherited from Old Spanish margen, marjen, margines, this form probably borrowed from Latin marginem. The form marcen (“strip of terrain in a field marked before sowing”) was likely inherited, however.
Inherited from Old Spanish marido, from Latin marītus.
Inherited from Latin marinus (“of the sea, marine”).
Inherited from Latin marīnus, from mare (“sea”), from Proto-Indo-European *móri.
Ultimately from Latin maritima, feminine of maritimus. Considering the Spanish word's /s/ and /i/, likely borrowed via Mozarabic. Compare Portuguese marisma, Catalan maresma, Italian maremma.
Probably from Latin malum folium (literally “bad leaf”).
Inherited from Old Spanish marruvio, from Latin marrubium.
From Latin marsūpium, from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion).

parole.significato: Tuesday (the third day of the week in many religious traditions, and the second day of the week in systems that use the…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish martes, from Latin Mārtis dīes, variant of diēs Mārtis.
Borrowed from Latin maritimus. Compare the inherited marisma.
Inherited from Old Spanish mas (“but”), from Latin magis. Doublet of más.
From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
Inherited from Latin massāre, from massa.
Inherited from Latin masticāre. Doublet of masticar, a borrowing. Cognate with English masticate.
Borrowed from Latin masticāre. The word mascar derives from the same source, but is a direct descendant while masticar is a later loanword. Cognate with English masticate.
Inherited from Old Spanish mastuerço, from Latin nasturtium. Doublet of nasturcio. The variant nastuerzo is influenced by the word's Latin etymon.
By surface analysis, matar (“kill”) + -dor (agent suffix). May correspond to Latin mactātōrem (“slayer, killer, slaughterer”), but the origin of the base verb matar is disputed.
From Latin mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, learning”).

parole.significato: matter (the basic structural component of the universe)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin māteria. Doublet of the inherited madera.
Borrowed from Latin mātrīcem, from māter (“mother”), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”).
Borrowed from Latin mātrōna (“matron”), from māter (“mother; matron”).
Borrowed from Latin maiusculus. Cognate with English majuscule.
Uncertain if inherited or semi-borrowed from Latin magnus (“big, large”), from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, from *méǵh₂s (“great”). Doublet of magno.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin meā culpā.
Inherited from Latin mēiere, reinterpreted in Vulgar Latin as a first-conjugation verb (*mēiāre). Compare Portuguese mijar and English micturate.
Inherited from Latin miscēre. Compare Portuguese mexer.
From Latin mēcōnium (“opium; excrement of a newborn child”), from Ancient Greek μηκώνιον (mēkṓnion, “poppy-juice, opium”), from μήκων (mḗkōn, “poppy”).
From Latin mēchanicus, from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós).
Inherited from Latin mēta. Doublet of meta.

parole.significato: half (one of two equal parts of any whole)
mediator (one who negotiates between parties seeking mutual agreement)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mediālis. Cf. also meaja.
Borrowed from Latin mediānus. Compare Old Spanish mejana.
From Old Spanish melezinamiento, from Latin medicāmentum. First attested in 1490.
Borrowed from Latin medicāre (“to cure, heal”).
Borrowed from Latin medicīna. Compare the form melecina.
From Latin medicīnālis. By surface analysis, medicina + -al.

parole.significato: half (of or related to one of two equal divisions of a whole)
parole.testo: Borrowed directly from Latin medius (“half”) rather than inherited through an Old Spanish form, possibly because the likely forms *meo and *meyo would have closely resembled mear (“to piss”), ultimately from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare Portuguese meio
Inherited from Latin mētīrī, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁-.
Borrowed from Latin meditābundus, from meditor (“meditate”) + -bundus.
Borrowed from Latin mephīticus, from mephītis.

parole.significato: an islet in a river; an eyot
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin mediāna (“middle”), but via Aragonese or Catalan (cf. mitjana).

Inherited from Latin melior, meliōrem (whence English ameliorate), from Proto-Indo-European *mélyōs, from *mel- (“strong, big”). Cognate with Portuguese melhor, Galician mellor, Catalan millor, French meilleur, Italian migliore.
Borrowed from Latin melēna, from Ancient Greek μέλαινα (mélaina, “black”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mālum cotōnium (“quince”), with influence from melón. Like quinces, peaches have a cottony fruit skin.
From Latin melōdia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδία (melōidía), from μέλος (mélos, “song”).
From Latin Melchita, from Byzantine Greek Μελχίτης (Melkhítēs), from Classical Syriac ܡܠܟܝܐ (malkāyāʾ, “royal; royalist”) + Byzantine Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). See these for more.

Inherited from Old Spanish membrillo, menbriello (c. 1250), from Latin melimēlum (“sweet apple”), via an intermediary Vulgar Latin *melimellum (according to Joan Coromines), from Ancient Greek μελίμηλον (melímēlon), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”). Compare Portuguese marmelo.

parole.significato: memory (the ability of the brain to record information)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish memoria (“memory”), from Latin memoria.

parole.significato: to turn the rope in the game of jump rope
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mināre, collateral form of minārī.

parole.significato: beggar (person who begs for a living)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish mendigo, from Latin mendīcus.

Inherited from Old Spanish menester, mester, inherited from Latin ministerium, with an irregular loss of the expected final -o. Coromines and Pascual explain this loss as due to being commonly found in the phrase es menester que, triggering syncope between -ter(o) and que, also arguing against the p

parole.significato: minor (person under the age of majority)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish menos, inherited from Latin minus, comparative of parum.

Arguably taken from Latin mēnsa (“table”); it is thought that medieval monks used the names of inanimate objects in disparaging reference to illiterate or non‐discerning people, partially out of a desire to not use an explicitly pejorative insult as would be forbidden by their canons.
From Latin mēnsuālis, variant of menstrualis.
From Latin menta, mentha (compare Catalan menta, French menthe, Italian menta), from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin mentem, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”). Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form miente.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin mente captus (literally “taken in the mind”).
Inherited from Old Spanish mentir (“to lie”), from Latin mentīrī.
Inherited from Latin minūtus (“small, little”). Doublet of minuto, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin mercātus. Doublet of marketa.
Inherited from Old Spanish merced, from Latin mercēdem (“pay, wage, reward”), from merx (“merchandise”), from Proto-Italic *merks.
Borrowed from Latin meretrīcius (“meretricious”), from meretrīx (“harlot, prostitute”), from mereō (“earn, deserve, merit”).
Borrowed from Latin merīdiem (“midday, noon”), as in the phrases ante meridiem and post meridiem (more commonly a. m. and p. m.).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin merenda. Compare Italian and Portuguese merenda.
Inherited from Latin mēnsis (“month”). Compare Catalan mes, Italian mese, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais.
Inherited from Latin mixtus. Doublet of mixto.
From Latin mānsiōnem, with metathesis of "i"; perhaps through French maison, or influenced by it. Doublet of mansión.
Borrowed from Latin meta (“turning spot in arena; goal”). Doublet of meda.

From Latin metamorphōsis, from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis), from μεταμορφόω (metamorphóō, “to transform, change, disguise”), from μετά (metá, “concerning change”) + μορφόω (morphóō, “to form”).

Inherited from Old Spanish meter, from Latin mittere (“to send”). The semantic shift from "send" to "put" probably occurred in Vulgar Latin. Cognate with English mess and also mission, message. Compare also French mettre, Friulian meti, Portuguese meter, and Italian mettere.
From Latin metopa, from Ancient Greek μετόπη (metópē).

parole.significato: metaphor (the use of a word or phrase to refer to something other than its literal meaning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).
Borrowed from Latin mīca. Compare the inherited doublet miga.

parole.significato: to pay a tax or other tribute

Inherited from Latin piscīna. Doublet of piscina.

parole.significato: pectoral (of or relating to the breast or chest)

From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós).
From earlier pedrenal, from Latin petrinus (from petra (“stone”)), with the suffix -al.
Borrowed from scientific Latin pedicellus (“small foot”), from pediculus, diminutive of pes.

parole.significato: a jump or leap given by pushing off and landing with a single foot.

parole.significato: order (request for some product or service or that which is requested)

Inherited from Old Spanish pena, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).

parole.testo: From Latin penātēs, from penus (“food provisions stored inside”).

parole.significato: to cross oneself, (make the sign of the cross over oneself)
person (an individual; usually a human being)

parole.significato: terebrant; resembling the sensation of being bored into or pierced.

parole.significato: to perturb, to disturb, to bother
