Inherited from Old Spanish prea, from Latin praeda. Doublet of presa.
Borrowed from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus.
Borrowed from Latin precārius. Doublet of plegaria.
From Latin praeceptīvus, from praeceptum. By surface analysis, precepto + -ivo.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin pretium. Doublet of prez.
Borrowed from Latin pretiōsus. By surface analysis, precio + -oso.
Borrowed from Latin praecipitāre (“to cast down, to throw headlong”).
Inherited from Old Spanish preciso, a learned borrowing from Latin praecīsus.
Borrowed from Latin praecox. Doublet of albaricoque.

parole.significato: precursory (relating to events that will follow)

parole.testo: From Latin praedīcere. Equivalent to pre- + decir.
Borrowed from Latin praedictivus, from praedico.
Borrowed from Latin praedīlēctiō. Compare French prédilection.
Borrowed from Latin praeferre, with a change of conjugation. Cognate with English prefer.
Inherited from Latin praecōnārī, a verb based on praecō (“herald, town crier”).

parole.significato: to eat a meal, generally before an important person, in order to check if it's poisoned

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pregon, from Latin praecōnem. Compare Portuguese pregão.
Borrowed from Latin praeiudicium. Doublet of perjuicio. Cognate with English prejudice.
From Latin praeiudicāre; probably an adaptation to Spanish juzgar. Compare French préjuger. Cf. also the doublet perjudicar. Cognate with English prejudge.
Borrowed from Latin praemium. Doublet of premium.
Inherited from Old Spanish premer, from Latin premere.

parole.significato: premise (either of the first two propositions of a syllogism, from which the conclusion is deduced)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praemissa, feminine of praemissus (“sent forth or forward or ahead”), perfect passive participle of praemittō (“to send forth or forward or ahead”).

parole.significato: to show beforehand; to guide, direct

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pendra, peñdra (with metathesis), from péñora, from Latin pignŏra, plural of pignus (“pledge; hostage”).
From older pendrar, from Latin pignorāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish prender, from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere.
From Latin pressāre (“to press”), from premo (“to press”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prehēnsiōnem. Doublet of prisión.

parole.significato: to worry, to concern, to trouble, to be worrisome to, to preoccupy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupāre (“to preoccupy”). Cognate with English preoccupy.

parole.significato: to predominate, to dominate, to prevail
to put or place in front of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praepōnere. By surface analysis, pre- + poner.
From Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), feminine of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).
From Latin presbyterātus, from on presbyter (“elder, presbyter”).
Borrowed from Latin presbyterī, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros, “elder”). Doublet of preste.
From Latin praescindō, formed from Latin prae- (“before”) + scindō (“split, divide”). Equivalent to pre- + escindir.
Inherited from Old Spanish presea (1250), from Latin praesidia, plural of praesidium (“protection, escort”).

parole.significato: to have a feeling, have a premonition; to be aware of
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praesentīre. By surface analysis, pre- (“before”) + sentir (“to feel”).
Learned borrowing from Latin praesidentem (“presiding over; president, leader”). By surface analysis, presidir + -ente. Doublet of president.
Learned borrowing from Latin praesidium. Doublet of the dialectal presillo, which was inherited.
Inherited from Latin praesidium, after following the sporadic [dj] > [ʎ] palatalization (as in omezillo). Doublet of presidio, which was borrowed.

Inherited from Old Spanish prestar, from Latin praestāre. Coromines and Pascual mention an old attestation of Latin praestō meaning "to lend" in a legal document of 438, the Interpretationes Theodosianae, where commodō is switched for praestō. This meaning is also attested in the Reichenau Glosses.
Borrowed from Latin praestigium. Cognate with Catalan prestigi, French prestige, Italian prestigio, Portuguese prestígio.
Borrowed from Latin praesumptivus. By surface analysis, presunto + -ivo.
From Latin praesūmptus, perfect passive participle of praesūmō.
Borrowed from Latin praevāricātiōnem (“collusion with an opponent; transgression; deceit”).
Borrowed from Latin praevāricātor, corresponding to prevaricar + -dor.
From Latin praevāricārī. Cognate with English prevaricate.

parole.significato: to prevent, to forestall, to preempt, to ward off, to stave off

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praevidēre. By surface analysis, pre- + ver. Cognate with English preview.
From Latin priapismus, from Ancient Greek πριαπισμός (priapismós), derived from Πρίαπος (Príapos, “Priapus”).
Borrowed from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primero.
Borrowed from Latin prīmātem (“first, principal; hero”).

parole.significato: first gear (lowest gear in a motor vehicle)
former (in contrast to the latter), first, first one
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish primero (“first”), from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primario.
Borrowed from Latin prīmus (“first”), from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos (“foremost”, superlative of pri, "before, in front").
From Latin prīmōrdiālis (“of the beginning”). Cognate with English primordial.
Inherited from Old Spanish prinçipal, principal, borrowed from Latin principālis.

parole.significato: prior (a high-ranking member of a monastery)

parole.testo: From Old Spanish priesa, from Latin pressa. Cognate with Sicilian prexa ~prescia.
Inherited from Old Spanish prisco, from Latin persicum (“peach”) (after metathesis).

parole.significato: prison (a place or institution of confinement, especially of long-term confinement for those convicted of serious crime…
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin prehēnsiōnem. Cf. French prison, Portuguese prisão. Doublet of prensión.
Inherited from Latin prīvātus (“bereaved; set apart from”).

parole.significato: to privatize (release government control to private industry)

parole.testo: A recent Latinism, borrowed from Latin prō; see above. Doublet of por.
Borrowed from Latin pro memoria (literally “for memory”).
Inherited from Old Spanish provar, from Latin probāre.

parole.significato: problem, issue, challenge (a difficulty or obstacle that has to be dealt with)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”).
Borrowed from Latin procācem (“bold, shameless, impudent”).

Borrowed from Latin prōcessiōnem (“a marching forward, an advance”), in Late Latin "religious procession" (genitive singular prōcessiōnis), from prōcessus, perfect passive participle of prōcēdō (“move forward, advance, proceed”).
Borrowed from Latin prōcessus, perfect passive participle of prōcēdō (“to advance, proceed”). Doublet of procés.
From Latin prodigalitātem. Cognate to Italian prodigalità.

parole.significato: prodigy (an especially gifted or talented person)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin productiōnem, equivalent to producir + -ción. Cognate with Catalan producció, Galician produción.
Borrowed from Latin productor, from productus.
From Latin prooemium, from Ancient Greek προοίμιον (prooímion).

parole.significato: profane; unholy (desecrating a holy place or thing)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía).

parole.significato: to utter, let out (especially an insult, curse, sigh or exclamation)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish propheta, a learned borrowing from Latin prophēta, borrowed from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs), from προ- (pro-, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to say”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix).
Borrowed from Latin profunditātem; equivalent to profundo + -idad. Cognate with Galician profundidade.

parole.significato: deep (having a bottom far from the surface or mouth)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin profundus. Cf. hondo.  PIE word  *bʰudʰmḗn
From Latin prophēticus, from Ancient Greek προφητικός (prophētikós); equivalent to profeta + -ico.
From progreso, from Latin prōgredior (“to proceed”). Cognate with Portuguese progredir.
Borrowed from Latin prōgressus (“an advance”), from the participle stem of prōgredī (“to go forward, advance, develop”), from pro- (“forth, before”) + gradi (“to walk, go”).
From Latin prohibitiōnem, equivalent to prohibir + -ción.
From pro- + hijo (“son”) + -ar, from Latin prāre (“for”) + fīlius (“son”).
Borrowed from Latin prōlixus (“courteous, favorable”). Compare Catalan prolix, Portuguese prolixo.
Inherited from Old Spanish prometer, from Latin prōmittere (“to promise; to send forth”).
Borrowed from Latin prōminentem, present active participle of prōmineō (“jut out, to project”).
Inherited from Old Spanish promission, borrowed from Latin promissiōnem.

parole.significato: to promote, to pioneer, to advance, to foster, to further

parole.testo: From pro- + nombre, from Latin pronomen, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ντωνῠμῐ́ᾱ (ăntōnŭmĭ́ā).
From earlier propriedad, borrowed from Latin prōprietātem.
From Latin prŏpīnāre, from Ancient Greek προπίνειν (propínein).

parole.significato: to propose, to propound, to put forth, to put forward, to bring forward, to suggest
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōpōnere (“to set forth; to propose; to declare”). By surface analysis, pro- + poner. Cognate with English propose and propound.

parole.significato: to fight for, advocate, stand up for, defend

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōpositum (“that which is proposed”).
From Latin proscēnium, from Ancient Greek προσκήνιον (proskḗnion).
Borrowed from Latin prosequi, modeled after Spanish seguir.
From Latin prosōdia, from Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía), from πρός (prós, “to”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

From the Latin prosōpographia (“description of a person’s appearance; description of an individual’s life”), from the Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face, person”) + -γρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (-grăphĭ́ā, “writing, drawing”). Cognate with English prosopography.
Borrowed from Latin prospectus, perfect passive participle of prōspiciō.

parole.significato: to prosper, to thrive, to flourish

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōstibulum (“prostitute, whore”) (in Late Latin, “brothel, whorehouse”).
Borrowed from Latin prōtestārī (“to protest; to testify”), from prō + testor, from testis (“witness”).
Inherited from Latin prōfectus (“progress, success”). Cognate with English profit.

parole.significato: to provide, purvey, supply, equip, furnish

parole.testo: From Latin prōverbiālis. Equivalent to proverbio + -al
Borrowed from Latin providentiālis. By surface analysis, providencia + -al.
From provocar + -dor, or borrowed from Latin prōvocātor.

parole.significato: to cause or provoke, to prompt
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōvocāre. Cognate with English provoke.
Borrowed from Latin prōiectāre, frequentative of prōiciō (“thrust out”).
Borrowed from Latin prūdentia. Compare English prudence.
Derived from Latin prūdentem. Cognate with English prudent.
From Latin pruna, plural of prunum.
Learned borrowing from Latin prōdigus (“wasteful, lavish, prodigal”), from prōdigō (“to squander, waste; to use up, consume”), from prō- + agō (“to do, make, drive”).

parole.significato: neighbour (a person living on adjacent or nearby land)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin proximus. Doublet of próximo.
Borrowed from Latin proximus. Doublet of prójimo.
Learned borrowing from Latin psychē, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, breath”).
From Latin psȳchicus, from Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós).

parole.significato: Ptolemaic (of or pertaining to the Ptolemy dynasty of pharaohs)
parole.testo: From Latin Ptolemāicus from Koine Greek Πτολεμᾱϊκός (Ptolemāïkós) from Πτολεμαῖος (Ptolemaîos), a proper name derived from Epic Greek πτόλεμος (ptólemos), variant of Ancient Greek πόλεμος (pólemos, “battle, war”); equivalent to Ptolomeo + -ico.
From Latin pūbertās. Cognate with Galician puberdade.
Inherited from Latin pultes, plural of puls.
Inherited from Latin potentem. Doublet of potente, which was borrowed.
Deverbal from poblar (“to populate”), inherited from Latin populāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish pueblo, from Latin populus (“people, nation”), from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”).

parole.significato: bridge (construction spanning a waterway, ravine, or valley from an elevated height)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish puente, from Latin pontem. Compare Catalan pont, French pont, Italian ponte, Occitan pònt, Portuguese ponte, Romanian punte, Romansh punt.

Inherited from Old Spanish puerco, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”). The "police officer" slang sense is apparently a semantic loan from English pig.
Inherited from Old Spanish [Term?], from Latin porrum. Compare the borrowed doublet porro, borrowed through Catalan.

parole.significato: door (portal of entry into a building)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish puerta, from Latin porta.

From the feminine of the past participle of the verb poner (puesto), from Latin posita, from the feminine of positus, perfect passive participle of ponō. Cognate with English posit, English post, and Italian posta.
Past participle of poner (“to put”); from Latin postus, from positus. Compare English post.
From Latin pugnāre. Doublet of puñar.
Inherited from Old Spanish puxar, from Latin pulsāre, frequentative of pellō. Doublet of pulsar, a borrowing. Compare English push.
From Latin pulchrum, accusative form of pulcher.
Inherited from Old Spanish pulgar, from Latin pollicāris, from pollex.
Inherited from Old Spanish pulmon, a borrowing from Latin pulmōnem, pulmō (“lung”), from Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō.

Inherited from Latin polypus (“cuttlefish, polyp”) (compare Catalan polp, pop, French poulpe, Galician polbo, Italian polpo, Portuguese polvo), from a variant of Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous, literally “many footed”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pólipo.
Borrowed from Latin pulsāre. Doublet of the inherited pujar.
Inherited from Old Spanish pulso, polso (“pulse”), from Latin pulsus.
Borrowed from Latin punctiōnem. Compare punzón, an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin pungere. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish puñir.
Inherited from Old Spanish punto, from Latin pūnctum (“point”), from pungō (“to prick, puncture”). Cognate with Asturian puntu, Catalan punt Galician punto, Portuguese ponto.
Probably from Latin punctiōnem. Doublet of punción, which was borrowed.
From puro + -eza or descended directly from Latin pūritia; in either case, from pūrus (“pure”).
Borrowed from Latin purgātor. By surface analysis, purgar (“to bleed”) + -dor.
From Latin pūrgantem. By surface analysis, purgar + -ante.
Inherited from Old Spanish purgar, a learned borrowing from Latin pūrgāre (“to purge; to clean”).

Inherited from Old Spanish puro, from Latin pūrus. In the noun sense short for cigarro puro, a product to be smoked that is made – unlike the cigarette – of “tabaco puro, sin papel” (pure tobacco, without paper). Note that in Spanish the unqualified term cigarro can also refer to a cigarette.
From Latin pustulosus, from pustula (“inflamed sore”).

parole.significato: puerpera (a woman who has just given birth)

Inherited from Latin pugnāre. Doublet of pugnar.
Inherited from Old Spanish puñir, from Latin pungere. Replaced by the borrowed form pungir.

parole.significato: fist (hand with the fingers clenched or curled inward)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish punno, from Latin pugnus.
Inherited from Latin pampinus: 'tendril or leaf of a vine'. Compare Sicilian pàmpina.
Borrowed from Latin parvulus, diminutive of parvus.

parole.significato: patina (a colored coating as results from oxidation of bronze or copper)

parole.testo: From Latin pinnula, diminutive of pinna (“wing, feather”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin pertica. Doublet of percha.

parole.significato: a bird feather intended for writing

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pius (“pious, devout”). First attested 1444.

parole.significato: potion (“beverage with magical or medicinal powers”), apozem
parole.testo: Apheresis of apócima, from Latin apozema, from Ancient Greek ἀπόζεμα (apózema, “to extract by boiling”), from the root ζέω (zéō, “to boil, seethe”), q. v. Compare Portuguese apózema, English apozem.
From Latin poculum. Doublet of búcaro.
From Latin polypus. Doublet of pulpo.
Inherited from Latin pūmicem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poHi-m- (“foam”).
Borrowed from Latin pōmŭlum, a diminutive of pōmum (“stone fruit”). Compare Catalan pòmul, French pommette. Compare typologically Proto-Slavic *agodica, a diminutive of *agoda.
Borrowed from Latin porticus. Doublet of porche.

parole.significato: governmental institution in charge of collecting and storing grain in order to distribute it in times of need
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin positus. Doublet of puesto.
From Latin pulpitum. Doublet of pupitre.
From Latin pūnicus (“Punic”), from poenicus (“Phoenician”), from Ancient Greek Φοῖνιξ (Phoînix, “Phoenician”).
Learned borrowing from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra). Cf. the inherited Old Spanish forms pórpola (“purple cloth”), pórpora.
Inherited from Latin quid (“what”), but usurping all the roles of Latin quod. Cognate with English who.

parole.significato: to break, to snap, to shatter (to smash or rupture)
parole.testo: Through metathesis, from Latin crepāre (“crack, creak”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-. Compare English crevasse.
Inherited from Latin qu(i)ētus. Doublet of quieto, which was borrowed.

Inherited from Latin cremātiōnem, affected by the same change as Spanish quemar (q.v.) < Latin cremāre. Compare Portuguese queimação. By surface analysis, quemar + -zón. Doublet of cremación, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Old Spanish querella, borrowed from Latin querēlla (“complaint”), from queror (“to lament, complain”) (compare English quarrel).

parole.significato: to desire, to want, to want to
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin quaerō (“seek, look for, desire”). Cognate with English query.
Inherited from Old Spanish queso, from Latin cāseus.
Borrowed from Latin quid prō quō.
Inherited from Latin quĕm, accusative of quī, from Old Latin quei, from Proto-Italic *kʷoi, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, *kʷos.

parole.significato: live by the sword, die by the sword
parole.testo: Calque of Latin qui gladio ferit gladio perit. Literally, “he who kills by iron, dies by iron”.
From quiescente + -encia, or borrowed from Latin quiescentia.
Learned borrowing from Latin quiēscēns, quiēscentem.
Learned borrowing from Latin quiētus. Doublet of inherited quedo.
From Latin cyma (“sprout of a plant”), from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma).
Borrowed from Latin chimaera, from Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira, “she-goat, chimera”). Cognate with English chimera.
From Latin quīna, feminine singular of quīnus (“fivefold”).
Inherited from Latin quīngentōs, from quīnque (“five”).
Borrowed from Latin quīnquennium, from quīnque (“five”) + annus (“year”).
From Latin quīnquerēmis (“5-oared”), from quīnque (“five”) + rēmus (“oar”) + -is (“forming compound adjs”).

From Latin quintana – cognate to English quintain (“a street between the fifth and sixth maniples of a Roman military camp, where warlike exercises took place”) –, the feminine of quintanus (“fifth-ranking”), from quintus (“fifth”), q.v.
Borrowed from Latin quinta essentia (literally “fifth element”).

parole.significato: one of the roads of the Roman camp
parole.testo: From Latin quintana (“the fifth”), giving name to one of the roads of the Roman camp where people used to sell groceries. Meaning of "homestead" in Asturias taken from Asturian quintana.

From Latin quintus. Pushed out Old Spanish cinquén(o), quintén(o) in line with the re-Latinization of many other numerals – compare Ladino sinkeno. From Latin chimicus, alternative form of chēmicus (“chemical”), from chēmia (“chemistry”), Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”).

parole.significato: Chian (of, from or relating to the island of Chios, North Aegean Region, Greece)
parole.testo: From Latin Chius, from Ancient Greek Χῖος (Khîos).
Borrowed from Latin rhabdomantīa. Equivalent to rabdo- + -mancia
From rabia + -ar, from Latin rabiēs. Cognate with Latin rabiō but not its descendant.
Inherited from Old Spanish rabo, from Latin rāpum (“turnip”). Cognate with English rape as in rapeseed the plant.
Inherited from Latin racēmōsus. By surface analysis, racimo + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Latin ratiōnem. Doublet of razón and ratio.
Borrowed from Latin radiantem. Cognate with English radiant.
Borrowed from Latin radiāre. Doublet of rayar.

parole.significato: to root (to take root and begin to grow)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rādīcāre. Doublet of arraigar.
Borrowed from Latin radius. Doublet of rayo.
Inherited from Old Spanish raer, from Latin rādere.

parole.significato: to till earth in preparation for spring planting

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ralo, from Latin rārus. Doublet of raro.
Inherited from Old Spanish ramo, from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Italic *wrād-mo-, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂dmos, from *wréh₂ds (“root”).
Inherited from Latin ramōsus. Equivalent to ramo + -oso.
Borrowed from Latin rapācem (“who robs, plunders”).
Borrowed from Latin rhapsōdia, from Ancient Greek ῥαψῳδία (rhapsōidía), from ῥάπτω (rháptō, “to stitch, to sew”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Borrowed from Latin raptāre, frequentative of rapio, rapire, whence the inherited Old Spanish rabir.
Borrowed from Latin rārus. Doublet of the inherited ralo.

Probably an alteration of Old Spanish resgar (with influence from rascar), itself likely from Latin resecāre; cognate to English resect, cf. also rasguñar ("to scratch and sketch"). Likely a doublet of resecar.

parole.significato: satin (cloth woven from silk, nylon or polyester with a glossy surface and a dull back)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish raso, from Latin rāsus, perfect passive participle of rādō, whence English raze.

From rastro + -illo (diminutive suffix). Or from an alteration of older rastillo (influenced by rastro), itself from Latin rāstellus, diminutive of rāstrum. Compare Italian rastrello, Portuguese rastelo, French râteau.
Inherited from Latin rāstrum. Compare English raster.

From Latin rāta (“considered, established, certain”, adjective) through ellipsis of phrases such as rāta parte (“established part”), rāta ratiōne (“established ration”) etc., feminine ablative singular of ratus, perfect active participle of rērī (“to think, judge, consider”). Learned borrowing from Latin ratiō. Doublet of ración and razón.

parole.significato: a while, bit (a short period of time)

Cf. the evolution of Latin cubitum > Old Spanish cobdo > modern codo, where the /u̯/ was absorbed into the preceding rounded v

* From Latin radiāre. Equivalent to rayo + -ar. Doublet of radiar. Cognate with English radiate. * (drive crazy): Of when a phonograph record (or a compact disc) got scratched (broken record) and repeats the same fragment over and over again.
Inherited from Old Spanish, inherited from Latin radius. Doublet of radio, a borrowing.
Inherited from Old Spanish raçon, inherited from Latin ratiōnem. Doublet of ración and ratio.
Inherited from Latin rādīcem, from Proto-Italic *wrādīks, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds. Cognate with English radish.
From Latin re-. The use with adjectives is typical of Ibero-Romance. Compare Italian stra- (from Latin extra-), French très (from Latin trans-; now spelt separate, but formerly also a prefix).
From Latin reactivus, equivalent to re- + activo.
Inherited from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”), from rēx. Cognate with English regal and royal.
From Latin reālitātem, equivalent to real + -idad. Doublet of reality.
Borrowed from Latin rebellis, with the -ld- arising from the effort of pronouncing a double Latin -ll- at the time (cf. celda).
Probably from Latin re- (“back, backwards”) + capus (“"head", later in Romance "end"”) + āre (“verb-forming suffix”). Maybe semantically influenced by recaudar, recabdar (“to collect”).
From re- + calcar, or from Latin recalcāre.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain

Borrowed from Latin sarcophagus, from Ancient Greek σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos), from σάρξ, σαρκός (sárx, sarkós, “flesh”) + φάγος (phágos).
Borrowed from Latin satyrion, from Ancient Greek σατύριον (satúrion).
From Latin satisfactus > satisfacere > satis + facere.
Borrowed from Latin satrapīa, from Ancient Greek σατραπεία (satrapeía), from σατράπης (satrápēs). By surface analysis, sátrapa + -ia.
Inherited from Old Spanish salze, inherited from Latin salicem (“willow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥H-ik- (“willow”). Doublet of sarga. Compare Catalan salze, Italian salice, Romanian salcie.
Borrowed from Latin saxum. Compare Portuguese seixo (“pebble”) and Italian sasso (“stone”) (which were, unlike the Spanish word, inherited).
From Latin saxātilis, from saxum (“a rock”).
From Old Spanish sazon, inherited from Latin satiō, -ōnem (“sowing, planting”), from serō (“to sow”).
Probably inherited from Latin saniēs, Late Latin sania interpreted as the base of īnsānia (“unsoundness of mind”), Spanish ensañar.

Inherited from Old Spanish sabuco, from Latin sabūcus, variant of sambūcus. With the case of Spanish, it was influenced in Vulgar Latin by the suffix -uccus (hence the -c- instead of expected -g-). Compare Galician and Portuguese sabugo, Asturian sabú, Catalan saüc.

parole.significato: A reflexive or reciprocal pronoun: oneself, himself, herself, itself, yourself; themselves; yourselves; each other; one…
used instead of indirect object pronouns le and les before the direct object pronouns lo, la, los, or las
parole.testo: From Old Spanish ge (from Latin illī, compare Portuguese lhe, Italian gli), whose pronunciation shifted from /ʒe/ to /ʃe/ in Early Modern Spanish, at which point it was reanalyzed as /se/ (rather than shifting to /xe/ as expected).
Inherited from Latin sēbum, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sebōsus. By surface analysis, sebo + -oso.
Inherited from Old Spanish secar, from Latin siccāre. Equivalent to seco (“dry”) + -ar.
Inherited from Old Spanish seze, from Latin sēdecim.
Borrowed from Latin sēclūsus. Compare with English secluse.
Inherited from Old Spanish seco, from Latin siccus.
From Latin secrētum, supine of sēcernō (“separate, disjoin”).

parole.significato: said of a follower of someone else's opinion, opportunistic
parole.testo: From Latin sequāx (“following”). Cognate with Portuguese sequaz and Italian seguace.
Borrowed from Latin sequestrum (“a depository”), derived from sequester (“mediator, trustee”). By surface analysis, secuestrar + -o.
Borrowed from Latin saeculāris. Doublet of seglar.
Formed from Latin secundus, or borrowed from Latin secundāre. Doublet of segundar.

Inherited from Old Spanish sed, sede, set, from Latin sitis (“thirst”). Cognate with Aragonese sete, Asturian sede, Catalan set, French soif, Galician sede, Italian sede, Portuguese sede, and Romanian sede. Doublet of tisis (“phthisis”).

parole.significato: silk (fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish seda, from Latin sēta, monophthongized variant of saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”).
Borrowed from Latin sedāre (“to settle, to calm”).
Inherited from Old Spanish segar, from Latin secāre. Unrelated to secar (“to dry”), which is from Latin siccāre.
From Latin saeculāris. Doublet of secular.
Inherited from Latin secundus with, per Coromines, a 'semi-learned' treatment of the stressed vowel (*segondo would have been expected otherwise). Doublet of según. Related to seguir (“follow”).

parole.significato: a small axe similar to or also fulfilling the function of an adze, a scythe, a fascis, or even a spokeshave
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish segur, from Latin secūris.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin sēcūritātem. By surface analysis, seguro + -idad.
Inherited from Old Spanish seguro, from Latin sēcūrus.

Inherited from Old Spanish segund, segunt, inherited from Latin secundus with, per Coromines, a 'semi-learned' treatment of the stressed vowel (*segón would have been expected otherwise). Doublet of segundo. Related to seguir (“follow”).
Inherited from Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἕξ (héx), French six, Old English six (English six).
Inherited from Latin sigillāre. Compare Portuguese selar, Catalan segellar, French sceller, Italian suggellare. Cf. also the borrowed doublet sigilar.
Inherited from Old Spanish sello, seello, from Latin sigillum. Doublet of sigilo.
Inherited from Old Spanish selva, from Latin silva, from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”).

parole.significato: to plant (place a seed or plant in soil or other substrate in order that it may live and grow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sēmināre. Compare English seminate.
From Latin semestris (“six months”), from sex (“six”) + mensis (“month”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sēmicirculus. By surface analysis, semi- + círculo.
Attested since 1385. Borrowed from Latin semideus.
Probably from a derivative of Latin semen (“seeds”). Corominas proposes Vulgar Latin *sēminia, plural of *sēminium, through a Mozarabic xeminio.
Borrowed from Latin sēminālis. First attested in 15th c..

parole.significato: semis (a Roman coin worth half an as)
sice (the number six in a game of dice)

parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin senātus, from senex (“old”).
Inherited from Latin sēmita (“narrow way, footpath”).

Inherited from Old Spanish seños, sennos, sendos (first attested in Cantar de mio Cid, via an intermediary *senlos (see coyunda for a similar development), from Latin singulus. Compare with sencillo which was inherited via a diminutive of the same Latin root.
From Latin senectūtem. Cognate with Galician senectude.

parole.significato: Courtesy vocative used before someone's name, surname or title
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin senior. Doublet of señor.
Inherited from Old Spanish seno, from Latin sinus. Compare French sein, Italian seno, Romanian sân, Romansh sain.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sedentāre, from Latin sedēns, present participle of sedeō.
Borrowed from Latin sententia (“way of thinking, opinion, sentiment”).

parole.significato: sententious (tending to use aphorisms or maxims, especially given to trite moralising)
parole.testo: From Latin sententiōsus. By surface analysis, sentencia + -oso.
From Latin sentimentum; equivalent to sentir + -miento.
Inherited from Old Spanish sentir (“to feel”), from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”). Cognate with English scent.
From Latin sēparātus. By surface analysis, separar (“to separate”) + -ado.

parole.significato: to separate, to detach (to disunite from a group or mass; to disconnect)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin separāre. Cf. the inherited Old Spanish xebrar, exebrar, dessebrar.
Learned borrowing from Latin sēpia. Doublet of jibia.
Semi-learned modification of earlier setiembre, based on the Latin septembrem.
Inherited from Old Spanish sepulcro, borrowed from Latin sepulcrum.

parole.significato: the act or state of burial
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sepultūra. Cognate with English sepulture.
From serba, from Latin sorba, plural of sorbum.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin serēnitātem. By surface analysis, sereno + -idad.
From Latin sēricum (“silk”) (from Ancient Greek Σήρ (Sḗr)) + cultura.

parole.significato: series (a number of things that follow one another)

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sērōtinus (“late (ripening); evening”) (after metathesis).

parole.significato: snake, serpent (legless reptile of the sub-order Serpentes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish serpiente, from Latin serpentem. Doublet of sierpe. Cognate with English serpent.
Inherited from Old Spanish serrar, from Latin serrāre.
Inherited from Latin sērōtinus. The metathesis of /dn/ is regular, compare candado.
Borrowed from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, French service, Norman sèrvice).
Inherited from Old Spanish seruidumne, inherited from Latin servitūdinem, derived ultimately from servus (“slave, servant”). Compare Portuguese servidão. By surface analysis, siervo + -dumbre.

parole.significato: to serve (to be a servant or worker; to render service)

parole.testo: From Latin servitūtem, probably a borrowing.

parole.significato: sixty (the cardinal number occurring after fifty-nine and before sixty-one, represented in Roman numerals as LX and in…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish sessaenta (“threescore”), from Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).

parole.significato: sesma, half-foot (a traditional unit of length, equivalent to about 13.9 cm)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sexta (“sixth”), altered by analogy with septima (“seventh”). Doublet of sexto and siesta. In related to the unit of length, from forming one-sixth of the vara (Spanish yard or rod).
Inherited from Old Spanish setaenta, from Latin septuāgintā, from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”). Doublet of Septuaginta.
Inherited from Latin saeptum, perfect passive participle of saepiō (“to enclose”). Doublet of septo.
From Latin sextum. By surface analysis, sexto + -eto.

Learned borrowing from Latin sextus, along with several other ordinal numerals (segundo, quinto, séptimo), a tendency shared with many other Romance languages. Compare the inherited feminine doublets, sesma and siesta.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin signa, plural of signum. Compare Catalan senya and English sign.
From seña + -ar, possibly corresponding to Latin signāre, and therefore a doublet of signar.
Learned borrowing from Latin sȳcophanta (“informer, trickster”), from Ancient Greek συκοφάντης (sukophántēs).
Borrowed from Latin sȳcomorus, from Ancient Greek σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + μόρος (móros, “black mulberry”).
Borrowed from Latin sīderālis, from sīdus (“star”).

parole.significato: Sidonian (of, from or relating to the city of Sidon, South Governorate, Lebanon)

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish siempre~sienpre, inherited from Latin semper. Compare Catalan sempre and Portuguese sempre.
From Latin sempervīvum, equivalent to siempre + viva.

Inherited from Old Spanish sierpe, from Latin serpēns, apparently via the nominative form, perhaps remodeled into a Vulgar Latin *serpēs, *serpem. Ultimately from Latin serpere (“slither, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. Cf. Spanish pavo (“turkey”) and gorgojo (“weevil”) for other animal na
Inherited from Old Spanish sieruo, from Latin servus (“servant, slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser-wo- (“guardian”), or perhaps of Etruscan origin.

parole.significato: siesta (a nap, especially an afternoon one taken during the hottest part of the day in some cultures)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish siesta, from Latin sexta (hora) (“sixth hour; noon”), feminine of sextus (“sixth”). Doublet of sexto and sesma. Cognate with Catalan and Portuguese sesta.
Inherited from Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá), Italian sette, French sept, Portuguese sete, Old English seofon (English seven).
From Latin sīphōnem, from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”), of unknown ultimate origin.
Borrowed from Latin sigillāre, from sigillum. Doublet of sellar.
Borrowed from Latin sigillum, a diminutive of signum. Doublet of the inherited sello. Cognate with English sigil and seal.
Inherited from Old Spanish sieglo, siglo, siclo, a semi-learned term derived from Latin saeculum (the expected popularly inherited result would be *sejo or *siejo).
Borrowed from Latin signāre. Compare also señar, which may be an inherited doublet.
From Latin signifĭcantem, equivalent to significar + -nte.

Inherited from Old Spanish syguiente, from the old present participle of seguir. Corresponds to Latin sequentem (“following”), the present active participle of sequor (“to follow”), from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare English sequential.

Inherited from Old Spanish silvar, siblar, from Latin sībilāre, with syncope of short /i/ and metathesis of /l/. Doublet of chiflar, which came through a Vulgar Latin variant form. Cognate with English sibilate.
From Latin Sīlēnus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνός (Sīlēnós).

Inherited from Old Spanish siella (“chair, saddle”), from Latin sella. Cognate with Asturian and Leonese siella (“chair”), Catalan sella (“saddle”), French selle (“saddle”), Galician and Portuguese sela (“saddle”), Italian sella (“saddle”), and Romanian șa (“saddle”); as well as distantly English sa
From Latin syllabĭcus, from Ancient Greek συλλαβικός (sullabikós), equivalent to sílaba + -ico.

parole.significato: symmetry (correspondence on either side of a dividing line, plane, center or axis)
parole.testo: From Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).
Inherited from Old Spanish simiente, semiente, from Latin sēmentis, from sēmen (“seed”).
Borrowed from Latin sīmius. Compare jimio, jimia, Old Spanish ximia.
Borrowed from Latin sympathīa, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia, “community of feeling”).
Borrowed from Latin symposion (literally “banquet”), from Ancient Greek συμπόσιον (sumpósion).
From Latin simulācrum, from the verb simulare (“to simulate”).
From Latin simulātor. By surface analysis, simular + -dor.
Borrowed from Latin simulāre. Doublet of semejar.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin sine diē (literally “without a day”).
Borrowed from Latin sine cūrā (“carefree”, literally “without care”).
Borrowed from Latin symphōnia. Doublet of zampoña and zanfonía.
Borrowed from Latin singulāris. Doublet of señero.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin pluralia tantum.
Learned borrowing from Latin singultus. Compare the inherited doublet sollozo.
Borrowed from Latin signum. Doublet of signo, cf. also seña. Cognate with English sign.
Borrowed from Latin synōnymus, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”). By surface analysis, sin- + -ónimo.
From Latin sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx).
From Latin Syrius, from Ancient Greek Σύριος (Súrios).
Inherited from Latin servientem. Doublet of sargento, taken from French.
Borrowed from Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organized whole, body”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Borrowed from Latin sīstrum. First attested in 1555.
Borrowed from Latin situs, perfect passive participle of sinō.
Inherited from Latin sub, from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo.
Inherited from Latin sub-. Doublet of sub-, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin superbia, with the /j/ raising, and blocking the diphthongization of the stressed vowel.
Inherited from Latin superbus, with influence from Spanish soberbia. Compare nervio, Old Spanish niervo.
Borrowed from Latin subōrnāre and perhaps adapted to the native prefix so-. Cognate with English suborn.

parole.significato: to be superfluous; to be left over or extra
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish sobrar, inherited from Latin superāre. Doublet of superar, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Old Spanish sobre, from Latin super (“above”), from *eks-uper, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out of”) (Latin ex) and *uperi (“above”), from *upo. Doublet of the borrowed super.
Inherited from Latin super-. Doublet of super-.

parole.significato: to cope with, to endure, to bear; to put up with
parole.testo: From a combination of Latin super and levāre, or from superelevāre, from elevāre, or from Spanish sobre- + llevar.
Inherited from Latin supernatāre. By surface analysis, sobre- + nadar.
Inherited from Latin superpōnere. Doublet of the borrowed superponer. By surface analysis, sobre- + poner.
From Latin superscrībere. By surface analysis, sobre- + escribir.

parole.significato: to come up, arise, come forth, be brought about
parole.testo: From Latin supervenīre (doublet of supervenir). By surface analysis, sobre- + venir.
Inherited from Old Spanish sobrevivir, from Latin supervīvere, equivalent to sobre- + vivir.
Inherited from Latin sobrīnus (“maternal cousin”). Compare Galician sobriño, Portuguese sobrinho.
From Latin sōbrius (“sober”), from se- (“without”) + ēbrius (“intoxicated”).
Inherited from Old Spanish socavar, socauar, probably from a Latin *succavāre, *subcavāre. Cognate with Portuguese socavar. By surface analysis, so- + cavar.

parole.significato: to socialize, teach about being sociable

parole.testo: From Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion, companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, ally”).
Borrowed from Latin societātem (“society, community”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, companion, ally”). The senses of "company" and "association" were later borrowings.
Borrowed from Latin socius (“partaking, associated; partner, associate”).

parole.significato: to assist, to help, to succor, to aid
to suffocate, to stifle, to smother
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suffōcāre. Compare English suffocate.

From older sujuzgar, from Old Spanish sujudgar, from Latin subiugāre, and influenced by the verb juzgar (“to judge”), from Old Spanish judgar, from Latin iūdicāre. Compare the borrowed doublet subyugar.
Inherited from Latin sōl (“sun”). The Peruvian currency makes reference to the meaning "sun", but is a shortening from Latin solidus.
From Latin solve in the hymn for St. John the Baptist.
From Latin sōlācium, possibly through Old Occitan solatz.
Inherited from Old Spanish soldar, from Latin solidāre. Compare solidar (a borrowed doublet).
Inherited from Latin sōlitātem. Doublet of saudade, which was borrowed from Portuguese.
Inherited from Latin sōlitūdinem. By surface analysis, solo + -dumbre. Largely replaced by the borrowed doublet solitud.
From Latin sōlēn (“pipe, tube”), from Ancient Greek σωλήν (sōlḗn), + -oide.

parole.significato: to be accustomed to doing something, to do something on a regular basis, to do something usually or often
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish soler (“to use to”), from Latin solēre. Compare Catalan soler, Italian solere, Ladino soler and Portuguese soer (archaic).
Inherited from Latin sublevāre. Doublet of sublevar. By surface analysis, so- + levar.

parole.significato: to request, to ask for, to solicit

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin solidāre. Compare soldar (an inherited doublet).
Borrowed from Latin soli Deo (“(for) God only”).
From Latin sōliloquium, from sōlus (“alone”) + loquor (“to speak”).
Borrowed from Latin solium (“seat, chair; throne”).
Borrowed from Latin sōlitārius. See also the inherited doublet soltero.
Borrowed from Latin sōlitūdō. By surface analysis, solo + -itud. Compare soledumbre, which was inherited.
From soliviar (“to help lift from below”), from Latin *subleviāre.

parole.significato: to help lift or support something from below
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin *subleviāre, from sub- (“below”) + levis (“light”) + -āre (infinitive verb ending).
Inherited from Old Spanish solo, from Latin sōlus (“alone; sole; only”).
Inherited from Old Spanish solo, from Latin sōlum.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin sōlstitium, from sōl + sistō + -ium.

Inherited from Latin sōlitārius (“lonely”). Compare Portuguese solteiro, Catalan solter. See also the borrowed doublet solitario. Another theory, perhaps less likely, derives it from suelto, from Latin solutus (“unbound, released, free, at large”).
Borrowed from Latin solūtiōnem, from the verb solvō.
Derivative of Old Spanish somo, from Latin summus, whence the borrowing sumo. Other etymologies derive it from a Latin summārius.
Inherited from Latin submittere or summittere. Cognate with English submit. By surface analysis, so- + meter.
Borrowed from Latin somnolentus. Doublet of soñoliento. Cognate with English somnolent.

From a derivative of Latin mergus, with various theories existing on the intermediate form: one derives it from the variant form somorgujón, from a Vulgar Latin *merguliōnem, later influenced by Latin submergō (compare Portuguese mergulho, mergulhão, Galician mergullón, somorgullo, Leonese mergollón
From Old Spanish sonar, inherited from Latin sonō, -āre.
Inherited from Old Spanish sonido, a semi-learned descendant of Latin sonitus, by analogy with tronido, ruido, chirrido, rugido and other words with the suffix -ido.
Inherited from Latin subrīdentem, present active participle of subrīdeō (“to smile”). By surface analysis, son- + riente.

Inherited from Latin subrīsa, feminine of subrīsus, perfect passive participle of subrīdeō (“to smile”). According to Coromines and Pascual, first attested in the early 17th century. Displaced older sonriso (from Latin subrīsus, subrīsūs). By surface analysis, son- + risa.

Inherited from Latin subrīsus, perfect passive participle of subrīdeō. Less likely, according to RAE, from Old Spanish sonrisar. First attested before 1409 in a poem by Francisco Imperial (who likely died that year or before) in Cancionero de Baena.

parole.significato: soup (any of various dishes commonly made by combining liquids, such as water or stock, with other ingredients, such as…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin suppa (“sopped bread”), from Proto-Germanic *supô.
From sopa, originally meaning "bread bathed in soup" which then came to mean strike or hit. Derivation from súbito or from Latin subitus is folk etymology.

parole.significato: to bear, to endure, to withstand, put up with, tolerate, to stomach, to weather, to handle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin supportāre. First attested in the fifteenth century. Cognate with English support although divergent in meaning.
From Latin sopōriferum, accusative form of sopōrifer, derived from sopor (“sleep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swep- (“to sleep”).
Inherited from Old Spanish sorber, inherited from Latin sorbēre. Spanish forms showing the expected stem-vowel diphthongization do occur regionally.
Inherited from Old Spanish sordo, from Latin surdus, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”). Compare English surd.

parole.significato: to raffle, to raffle off, to draw lots
parole.testo: From Latin sortem. Compare English sort.
Inherited from Old Spanish sosañar, from Latin subsannāre.

parole.significato: to hold, to hold up, to prop up, to sustain, to underpin (physically)

parole.testo: From Latin saltāre. Doublet of saltar.
Inherited from Latin saltus (“forest or mountain pasture”).
From soñar + -dor, possibly corresponding to Latin somniātōrem. Compare Portuguese sonhador.
Inherited from Latin somnolentus. Doublet of somnoliento.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin statū quō (literally “in the state in which”), from statū, ablative singular of status (“state”), + quō (“in which”), ablative singular of quī (“which”).

parole.significato: stylus (plastic stick used for interacting with touchscreen devices)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin suadēre (“to advise, recommend”).
Borrowed from Latin sub-. Doublet of so-, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin sub hastā (literally “below the spear”), originally a mark of legal authority for the sale of spoils of war, later designating public auctions.

parole.significato: to go up or come up
parole.testo: From Old Spanish subir (borrowed, inherited form sobir), from Latin subīre (“approach”).
Inherited from Old Spanish subitaneo, borrowed from Latin subitāneus.
Borrowed from Latin subiunctīvus (“serving to join, connecting; of the subjunctive mode”), from subiungō (“to add, to join, to subjoin”), from sub- (“under”) + iungō (“to join”).
Borrowed from Latin sublevātiōnem, from sublevo.

parole.significato: to provoke into rebellion, to revolt
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sublevāre. Doublet of the inherited solevar.
Morphologically sub- (“under, below”) + Latin līmen (“threshold”) (genitive līminis) + -al (“adjective”).
Ultimately from Latin subrogāre. Cognate with French subroger, Italian surrogare.
From sub- + seguir, or borrowed from Latin subsequi, modeled after Spanish seguir.
From Latin subvenīre. Doublet of suvenir.
From Latin subiācentem. Cognate with English subjacent.
Borrowed from Latin subiugātiō. By surface analysis, subyugar + -ción.
Borrowed from Latin subiugāre. Compare the inherited sojuzgar.
Borrowed from Latin succinum, alternative form of sūcinum.

Borrowed from Latin sūctiōnem, attested since Late Latin and derived from sūgō (“to suck”). According to Coromines and Pascual, first attested in 1615, in a text by the medical writer Juan Sorapán de Rieros.

parole.significato: to happen, to befall, to occur
parole.testo: From Latin succēdere. The meaning of "to be successful" was lost from this verb and given to the verb conseguir and the verb phrase "tener éxito".

Inherited from Old Spanish suzio, from Latin sūcidus (“juicy; oily, greasy”), from sūcus (“juice, sap”) whence English succinite (“Baltic amber”). Compare Ladino suzio and English suck. For the sound change of the ending, compare limpio from Latin limpidus, and Old Spanish pudio from pūtidus.
Inherited from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin sūdōrem due to retention of d. The inherited term from Old Spanish suor coexisted with the early borrowing sudor until the latter displaced the former.
Inherited from Old Spanish suelo, from Latin solum (“floor; ground, soil”).
Inherited from Old Spanish sueno, from Latin sonus. Doublet of son.
Inherited from Old Spanish suerte, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Compare Portuguese sorte, Galician sorte.

Inherited from Old Spanish suenno, from Latin somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos. Compare Portuguese sono, Italian sonno (“sleep”) and Sicilian sonnu (“sleep”).
Inherited from Old Spanish suenno, from Latin somnium (“dream”), a derivative of somnus (“sleep”) (as Etymology 1). Compare Portuguese sonho, Italian sogno (“dream”) and Sicilian sonnu (“dream”).
Borrowed from Latin sufficientem, present participle of sufficiō.
Borrowed from Latin suffīxus, perfect passive participle of suffīgō (“to fasten; to fix onto”).
Borrowed from Latin suī generis (literally “of its (own) kind”).

parole.significato: to steady, hold, secure, attach, fasten
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin subiectāre (“to put under, to bring near”), frequentative of subiciō.

parole.significato: vision (something seen; an object perceived visually)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vīsiōnem, from vīsiō + -em. Cognate with Catalan visió.

parole.significato: to make out (to see something faintly or indistinctly due to distance or lack of light)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vitalitātem, equivalent to vital + -idad.
Borrowed from Latin vitella, diminutive of vitula.
From Latin vītis (“vine, grapevine”) + cultor (“cultivator, tiller”) (genitive singular cultōris).
Inherited from Old Spanish vitualla, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin vīctuālia.

Inherited from Old Spanish viuda, vibda, bibda, biuda, from Latin vidua, following metathesis. The Spanish word may have had some later influence from the Latin in the Middle Ages; compare the strictly popular Old Spanish form viuva, which is the form also found in Portuguese and Old Catalan, derivi

From Latin viduus (“widowed”), probably modeled on the feminine form viuda, which predated it. It may have been altered from an Old Spanish form vidu (itself a learned borrowing from Latin) due to influence from the feminine; a naturally inherited form would be viso, which was attested once in isola
Borrowed from Latin vivacitātem, equivalent to vivaz + -idad.
Inherited from Latin vīvārium, from vīvō (“to live”).
Inherited from Latin vivenda, feminine future participle of vīvō (“to live”). Compare Portuguese vivenda, Occitan vivenda; cf. also French viande (whence the Spanish doublet vianda was borrowed).

Inherited from Latin vīventem, accusative of Latin vīventem, the present active participle of vīvō (“live, be alive”). The same formation, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃wontm̥, is seen in Ashkun źit, Kamkata-viri ǰat, Sanskrit जीवन्त (jī́vanta), Waigali ǰit.
From Old Spanish bevir, bivir, vevir, viver, inherited from Latin vīvere. Compare Ladino bivir, Portuguese viver.

Inherited from Old Spanish bivo, vivo, from Latin vīvus. The dissimilated bivo was most common during the Middle Ages (compare Old Spanish bivir and bolver), with vivo becoming the standard form during the Spanish Golden Age for its semblance to the Latin etymon.
From Latin vivifĭcus, derived from vivax (“lively”).
Borrowed from Latin viāticum (“provision for a journey”), from the adjective viāticus (“pertaining to a journey”). Doublet of viaje.
Inherited from Old Spanish vinna, from Latin vīnea (“vineyard; grapevine”), a nominalization of vīneus (“of or relating to wine”), from vīnum (“wine”) + -eus.
Inherited from Latin vīnētum (“vineyard”), from vīnum (“wine”), influenced by viña.

parole.significato: vocation (inclination to undertake a certain kind of work)
to vociferate (to cry out with vehemence)

parole.testo: From Latin volatūra. By surface analysis, volar + -dura.
Inherited from Latin volāre. Doublet of volear. Compare Galician and Portuguese voar.

Likely a semi-learned word, which became well-ingrained in the popular language at an early date, taken from Latin voluntātem (cf. also Old Spanish form veluntad), accusative singular form of voluntās (“will, desire, disposition toward”); however, as no descendant of the related volō exists in Spani
Borrowed from Latin voluptuōsus, from voluptās (“pleasure”). Ultimately related to Latin volō (“to wish, to want”), therefore to English will.

parole.significato: to return, to revert, to get back
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin volvere (“roll, roll back”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vomitāre, frequentative of vomere (“spew”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vorāx, from vorō (“to devour”) + -āx (“inclined to”).
Borrowed from Latin vorāgine, singular ablative of vorāgo.

parole.significato: you, familiar form of the second-person singular pronoun
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vōs (“you, plural”), from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs.

parole.significato: you, you guys; second person plural personal pronoun
parole.testo: From older vos (“you”) (plural), from Latin vōs, and otros (“others”), plural of otro, from Latin alter (“other”). Compare Galician vosoutros, Catalan vosaltres, Occitan vosautres, French vous autres, Italian voialtri, Sicilian vuiautri.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin vōtum. See also boda.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin vōx populī.
Inherited from Old Spanish voz, from Latin vōcem. Sense 2 is presumably a semantic loan from Latin.
Inherited from Latin vostrum, from vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.

parole.significato: Vulcanian; of or relating to Vulcan, the Roman god of fire

parole.testo: From Latin Vulcānus (“Vulcano”), Roman god of fire + -logía.

Inherited from Old Spanish vulpeja, golpeja, gulpeja, from Latin vulpēcula, diminutive of vulpēs, from earlier volpēs, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl(o)p- ~ *h₂ulp- (“(red) fox”).
Borrowed from Latin vulpīnus.; compare vulpeja (“fox”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, from earlier volva, from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind”).

Valga in this context may be an archaism, inherited from an earlier expression in Spanish back when the language still retained some of the many meanings of Latin valere (“to be worth”), one of its meanings being "to be well, to be healthy". Spanish valer (“to be worth”) comes from that word. If so,
Borrowed from Latin validus (“healthy; valid”), from valeō (“to be healthy”).
From Latin Vandalus, named after the Germanic tribe, from Proto-Germanic *wandilaz.
From Latin vēlitēs, plural of vēles.
From Latin vertebra (“joint”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.
From Latin vertex. Doublet of vórtice.

parole.significato: Way of the Cross; Via Crucis
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin via crucis (literally “way of the cross”).
Inherited from Old Spanish biuora, from Latin vīpera (“viper”), a conflation of vīvus (“alive”) + pariō (“to give birth to”). Doublet of guiverno.

parole.significato: tie, bond (strong connection between people or groups of people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vinculum (“tie, bond”), from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -ulum. Doublet of brinco.
Borrowed from Latin viscera n pl, plural of viscus n (“internal organ”).

Inherited from Old Spanish viésperas (“evening, vespers, eve”), inherited from Latin vespera. For the lack of vowel syncope despite being an inherited word, compare áspero, níspero, miércoles. For the development of the stressed vowel, also compare avispa (from Old Spanish biespa).
Inherited from Old Spanish vitreo, a learned borrowing from Latin vitreus. Doublet of vidrio.
From Latin vortex. Doublet of vértice.
Inherited from Old Spanish é or e, from Latin et.

parole.significato: now, right now, (in the negative) anymore, no longer
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ya (“already; now”), from Latin iam. Compare Ladino ya, Asturian yá, Galician xa, Portuguese já, Catalan ja, French déjà, and Italian già.
Inherited from Old Spanish yazer, inherited from Latin iacēre, iaceō. Cognate with French gésir, Italian giacere, Portuguese jazer, Catalan jeure, Romanian zăcea. Compare English gist and joist.
Borrowed from Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).
Inherited from Old Spanish yegua, from Latin equa, feminine form of equus (“horse”).
Inherited from Old Spanish yema, inherited from Latin gemma. Doublet of gema.
Inherited from Old Spanish yerno, from Latin generum (“son-in-law”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.

parole.significato: any variety of bitter vetch (Vicia ervilia)
parole.testo: Syncopated from yervo, from Latin ervum.
Inherited from Old Spanish yesca, iesca, from Latin ēsca. Doublet of esca. Compare Portuguese isca.
Inherited from Old Spanish yesso, from Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γῠ́ψος (gŭ́psos). Doublet of aljez and gis, both through via Arabic.
Borrowed from Latin jejunum, ieiunum. Doublet of the inherited ayuno.

parole.significato: yoke (team of draft animals yoked together to pull a plow)
parole.testo: From yugo (“yoke”) + -ada (“-ful”), from Latin iugum. Compare Latin iugerum (“juger”).

parole.significato: yoke (bar or frame of wood by which two animals are joined)
parole.testo: From Old Spanish yugo, from Latin iugum, from Proto-Italic *jugom, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm, a root shared by iungō (“to join”). As it does not display the usual expected sound shifts from Latin, Meyer-Lübke considered it a semi-learned medieval borrowing, while Coromines and Pascual see it a
Borrowed from Latin iugulāre (“slay, slit throat”).

parole.significato: a pair or yoke of oxen
parole.testo: From yunto (“yoked”), from Latin iūnctus, past participle of iungō (“to yoke, to join”). Doublet of junta.
Borrowed from Latin iambicus, from Ancient Greek ἰαμβικός (iambikós), from ἴαμβος (íambos, “iamb”).
From za (alteration of Latin sub (“low”)) + abordar.
From Latin sapphīrus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros).

parole.significato: to criticize severely, harshly (to the point of feeling humiliated or mortified)
parole.testo: Somewhat disputed; according to the Royal Spanish Academy, from Old Spanish façerir, from *fazferir, from faz (“make!, do!”) + ferir (“to hurt”). However, many etymologists have suggested that faz in fazferir could not have turned into za(z), even if it did convert into haz during the Spanish conver
Inherited from Old Spanish çanpoña, from Latin symphōnia. Doublet of sinfonía and zanfonía.
Ultimately from Latin symphōnia, perhaps formed as a blend of the borrowed doublet sinfonía and the 'popular' zampoña.
From earlier cercillo, from Old Spanish cerciello, inherited from Latin circellus.
From Old Spanish ceda, from Latin zēta or its etymon, Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta).
From Latin zeugma, from Ancient Greek ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “bond, yoking”).
Borrowed from Latin zōdiacus, from Ancient Greek ζῳδιακός (κύκλος) (zōidiakós (kúklos), literally “circle of small animals”), from ζῴδιον (zōídion), a diminutive of ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).
Derived from Latin zōna (“girdle, zone”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē), from Proto-Indo-European *yoh₃snéh₂, from *yeh₃s- + *-néh₂.
Inherited from Latin soccus (“slipper”). Compare Catalan soc.

parole.significato: plinth, socle, base (a block or slab upon which a column, pedestal, statue or other structure is based)
parole.testo: From Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“slipper”).
Borrowed from Latin abacus, from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “a calculation board covered with sand”).
Inherited from Latin āfricus (“African”), referring to the origin of the wind. Doublet of áfrico.
Borrowed from Latin āfricus. Doublet of ábrego.
Borrowed from Latin agapē, from Ancient Greek ἀγάπη (agápē).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin achātēs, from Ancient Greek ἀχάτης (akhátēs).
Inherited from Latin alid, variant form of aliud, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos.

parole.significato: olive branch bent down and reaching the ground
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps Latin ālipēs (“winged”) or alapa (“blow, smack”). Compare Romanian aripă (“vane”).

parole.significato: album (a book designed to keep photographs, stamps, autographs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin album. Doublet of albo and obo.

parole.significato: decisive, critical, pivotal (of a moment or event)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin algidus (“very cold”), used in medical and poetic senses to describe coldness and stiffness. The figurative sense is perhaps derived from the frequently fatal algid stage of a fever (characterized by coldness as a result of shock). See also Italian algente (“cold”) and English al
Learned borrowing from Latin alibī (“elsewhere, at another place”).
Borrowed from Latin aloē, from Ancient Greek ἀλόη (alóē).
From Latin alsinē, from Ancient Greek ἀλσίνη (alsínē).
Borrowed from Latin ampulla. Doublet of ampolla.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin anatem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts (“duck”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ancora. Doublet of ancla.
Borrowed from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús).
Borrowed from Latin angelus Dominī (literally “the Lord's angel”), the prayer's opening words.
Borrowed from Latin anima. Compare alma, a doublet inherited from the same source.
Alteration of ánsar (“wild goose”), from Latin ānser (“goose”).
Borrowed from Latin anthrax, from Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax).
Borrowed from Latin apex. Doublet of ápice.
Borrowed from Latin apicem. Doublet of ápex.
Borrowed from Latin Arabs, from Ancient Greek Ἄραψ (Áraps, “Arab, Arabian”), from Arabic عَرَب (ʕarab).
Inherited from Old Spanish arbol, arbor, from Latin arborem f. Compare Portuguese árvore.
Borrowed from Latin area. Compare the inherited doublet era (“threshing floor”).

parole.significato: Arctic (of or relating to the Arctic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós, “northern, of the (Great) Bear”), from ἄρκτος (árktos, “bear, Ursa Major”).

Borrowed from Latin asperum, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”). The forms of the Spanish word and its Portuguese equivalent seem to indicate that they may be semi-learned or borrowed terms (the expected normal result aspro was found on rare occasions in Old Spanish documents). However, com
Borrowed from Latin aspis, aspidis, from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís).
Borrowed from Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).

parole.significato: atom (the smallest possible amount of matter which still retains its identity as a chemical element)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).
Borrowed from Latin avidus (“eager, desirous; greedy”), from aveō (“wish, desire, long for, crave”).
From Latin aegidem, from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís, “goatskin”) (from which the shield of Athena was made, and thus the sense “protection, shield”), from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”). First attested in 1589.
From Latin ecloga, from Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”).

parole.significato: he, him, masculine personal third person subject and disjunctive pronoun (used as a subject and after prepositions)
brazen; made of copper or bronze

parole.testo: From Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “appearance, significance, emphasis”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to show, present”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).
From Latin entasis, from Ancient Greek ἔντασις (éntasis, “tension, straining”), from ἐντείνω (enteínō, “to stretch or strain tight”).
Borrowed from Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós).
Inherited from Latin ipse. The slang sense to refer to a person is, allegedly from urban legend, from South Mexico and became popular slang in pachuco culture [1940s].

Learned borrowing from Latin ethica, from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
From Latin ethnicus, from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós).

Borrowed from Latin exitus (“exit, conclusion, result”), perfect passive participle of exeō (“to go out”). Doublet of ejido (“common land”). Cognate with English exit. The sense developed from “result” to “positive result”.
From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos).
From Latin extasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis), from ἐξίστημι (exístēmi, “to displace”) from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Borrowed from Latin ībicem (“chamois”), of Iberian origin.
Borrowed from Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”). Cognate with English idol.
From Latin igneus (“fiery, hot, on fire, burning; ardent, fervid, vehement”), from ignis (“fire”).
Learned borrowing from Latin īlĕus, from Ancient Greek εἰλεός (eileós), from εἰλῶ (eilô, “to twist”).
Borrowed from Latin incola (“inhabitant, resident”), from incolō (“to dwell, inhabit”).
Borrowed from Latin Indicus, from India, borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἰνδία (Indía), from Ἰνδός (Indós) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
Early variation of índico, from Latin indicus.
Learned borrowing from Latin integrum. Doublet of entero, which was inherited.
Learned borrowing from Latin obelus, from Ancient Greek ὀβελός (obelós).

parole.significato: obolus (a silver coin minted in Ancient Greece, valued at a sixth of a drachma)
parole.testo: From Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós).
Learned borrowing from Latin oculus. Doublet of ojo, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux).
From Latin opalus, from Byzantine Greek ὀπάλλιος (opállios), from Sanskrit उपल (upala, “gem, stone”).

parole.significato: organ (a larger part of an organism)
parole.testo: Probably a borrowing or semi-learned term from Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon). Compare the popular form found in place names like Boca de Huérgano.
Borrowed from Latin ōsculum (“kiss”), diminutive of ōs (“mouth”).
From Latin ulcera, plural of ulcus (“sore; ulcer; wound”), of uncertain origin.
